evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists valproic acid and sodium divalproate under Agents/circumstances to avoid for POLG-related disorders because of hepatic risk.

evidence.snippet: Patients with this disorder are at high risk of death from status epilepticus and from liver failure, if exposed to sodium valproate.
evidence.explanation: Direct clinical evidence of fatal valproate-associated liver failure in recessive POLG disease.

evidence.snippet: These findings implicate impaired liver regeneration in VPA toxicity and show that prospective genetic testing of POLG will identify individuals at high risk of this potentially fatal consequence of treatment.
evidence.explanation: Supports pre-treatment POLG genotyping to identify patients at high risk of valproate hepatotoxicity.

treatments/2.description: Valproic acid (Depakene) and sodium divalproate/divalproex (Depakote) must be avoided in all POLG-related disorders, including PEOB1, because they can precipitate or accelerate liver disease and fatal hepatic failure. This is not a theoretical caution: in a 26-patient recessive POLG cohort, liver failure caused or contributed to death in eight patients, all but one of whom were on valproate. The risk is genotype-driven and detectable prospectively, so POLG genotyping should precede valproate in anyone with a suspected mitochondrial or unexplained epilepsy phenotype. This record is curated with negative valence - the intervention is withholding the drug, not administering it.

evidence.snippet: monitoring of liver enzymes every three months or as clinically indicated; monitoring of epilepsy with repeat liver function tests after introduction of any new anti-seizure medication.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommendation for POLG-related disorders.

treatments/3.description: Liver enzymes should be monitored every three months or as clinically indicated, and liver function retested after introduction of any new anti-seizure medication - the surveillance counterpart of the valproate contraindication.

evidence.snippet: we assessed the safety and efficacy of combination therapy with deoxycytidine and deoxythymidine (dC/dT) in children with POLG-related disorders.
evidence.explanation: Phase 2 open-label trial of enteral dC/dT across POLG-related disorders. Cited PARTIAL for PEOB1 because the interim cohort was children with Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome and ataxia-neuropathy spectrum, not adult-onset recessive PEO.

evidence.snippet: During the 6 months of treatment, NMDS score improved from a mean of 27.3 at baseline to 20.7 at 6 months
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the primary efficacy signal. PARTIAL because it is an uncontrolled single-arm interim result in a mixed POLG cohort.

evidence.snippet: At present, there are no effective treatments for POLG-related disorders.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that no disease-modifying therapy is established for the POLG spectrum, which is why the rest of this section is supportive care.

treatments/4.description: Investigational, not standard of care. Enteral deoxycytidine plus deoxythymidine (dC/dT) aims to replenish the mitochondrial dNTP pool and so partially compensate for the reduced replication capacity of mutant polymerase gamma - the only curated treatment here that targets the causal mechanism rather than the consequences. An open-label single-arm phase 2 trial (NCT04802707) in POLG-related disorders reported improvement in the Newcastle Mitochondrial Disease Scale and stable-or-falling GDF-15 at 6 months. Important scope caveat for PEOB1: the interim cohort was children, six of ten with Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome and two with ataxia-neuropathy spectrum, so efficacy in adult-onset recessive PEO specifically is untested.

evidence.snippet: Once the POLG pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, testing for at-risk family members is possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews genetic counselling guidance for autosomal recessive POLG-related disorders.

treatments/5.description: Autosomal recessive counselling with a 25% sib recurrence risk, carrier testing for at-risk relatives once the familial variants are known, and the option of prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing. Counselling should explicitly cover the valproate contraindication for heterozygous relatives, who are at increased risk of valproate hepatotoxicity even though they do not develop PEO.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, our results showing that type IIB fibers in EOMs are affected earlier and more extensively (see Figs. 3A, 3B, 3E), suggest that these fibers might either have a faster rate of mitochondrial DNA deletion accumulation, clonal expansion, or a lower threshold compared to the other fiber types.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly leaves the three candidate mechanisms unresolved.

open_questions/0.rationale: Extraocular muscle carries a threefold higher burden of COX-deficient fibres than limb muscle in CPEO patients, and accumulates somatic mtDNA deletions faster during normal ageing. Candidate explanations - a lower heteroplasmy threshold, a faster deletion generation rate, more permissive clonal expansion, lower mitophagy efficiency, or fibre-type-specific mitochondrial fusion dynamics - have not been discriminated. This matters because the tissue-selectivity, not the enzymology, is what makes PEO a distinct clinical entity from the other POLG phenotypes carrying the same alleles.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, the clinical presentation was similar in siblings, implying a genetic basis for the phenotypic variability amongst homozygotes. However, the p.Ala467Thr allele was present on a shared haplotype in each affected individual, and there was no correlation between the clinical presentation and genetic variants in any of the analysed nuclear genes.
evidence.explanation: Documents both the evidence for a genetic modifier and the failure of the candidate-gene search to find one.

evidence.snippet: Our results suggest that the mitochondrial DNA background plays an important role in modifying the disease phenotype but nuclear modifiers, epigenetic and environmental factors may also influence the severity of disease.
evidence.explanation: States the residual uncertainty about which class of modifier dominates.

open_questions/1.rationale: 68 p.A467T homozygotes across eight centres span essentially the entire POLG phenotypic spectrum, and clinical presentation clusters within sibships, implying heritable modifiers. Yet a genome-directed search within POLG and its flanking regulatory regions, and in POLG2, TWNK/PEO1 and ANT1, found no correlating nuclear variant. The only signal identified was mitochondrial DNA haplogroup U, which was protective against epilepsy. So the modifiers that decide a PEO versus an Alpers presentation remain unidentified, and this is the central unsolved problem of POLG nosology - it is also why PEOB1 cannot be predicted from genotype alone.

evidence.snippet: Compound heterozygotes have a significantly more severe phenotype raising the possibility of a dominant negative effect.
evidence.explanation: Raises the dominant-negative hypothesis without testing it.

open_questions/2.rationale: Compound heterozygotes have significantly shorter survival than homozygotes for either allele, which is not what a simple additive loss-of-function model predicts. A dominant-negative mechanism was proposed but has not been tested biochemically - Pol gamma functions as a heterotrimer, so a poisoned-complex model is plausible but unproven. Resolving this would change how compound-heterozygote prognosis is counselled.

evidence.snippet: We report here a novel GJB2 mutation N54K segregating in a family with BPS, which was not detected in 110 control individuals of Northern European ancestry.
evidence.explanation: Segregation of the heterozygous N54K variant with BPS in the index family.

evidence.snippet: This non-conservative missense mutation lies within a cluster of pathogenic GJB2 mutations affecting the evolutionary conserved first extracellular loop of Cx26 important for docking of connexin hemichannels and voltage gating.
evidence.explanation: Places the BPS allele in the first extracellular loop and names the domain's function.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion is a heterozygous missense substitution in the evolutionarily conserved first extracellular loop of connexin 26, the domain that mediates hemichannel docking and voltage gating. p.Asn54Lys segregated with BPS in the family in which the gene was identified; p.Gly59Ser has been reported in BPS and in classic Vohwinkel syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The N54K mutant formed very few plaques and remained in an endoplasmic reticulum-like distribution pattern
evidence.explanation: Trafficking and plaque-localization result in Cx30-coexpressing HeLa cells.

evidence.snippet: The dominant syndromic Cx26 mutant N54K had trafficking defects and did not fully prevent wild-type Cx26 gap junction plaque formation but surprisingly formed gap junctions when co-expressed with Cx30.
evidence.explanation: N54K plaque localization improved with Cx30 in HEI-OC1 cells. The functional FRAP experiments tested S183F, not N54K/Cx30, so functional rescue was not shown.

steps/2.description: N54K connexin 26 is predominantly intracellular, partially colocalizing with an endoplasmic-reticulum marker in HeLa cells and forming few plaques. This is cell-context dependent: Cx30 coexpression recruited N54K into membrane plaques in HEI-OC1 cochlear-derived cells. That study measured localization, not restoration of N54K channel function. Patient skin immunostaining is a separate observation and does not demonstrate intracellular retention.

evidence.snippet: Cells expressing either the N54K or S183F mutants were essentially unable to establish gap junction channels capable of dye transfer
evidence.explanation: N54K alone in connexin-deficient HeLa cells lacks detectable dye coupling.

evidence.snippet: However, the N54K mutant abolished the functional gap junctional status of co-expressed Cx26, as assessed by the ability to pass a fluorescent dye
evidence.explanation: Dominant-negative effect on wild-type Cx26 in the HeLa assay.

steps/3.description: N54K expressed alone in connexin-deficient HeLa cells fails to support gap-junction dye transfer. Coexpression with wild-type Cx26 can restore some plaque localization while dye transfer remains absent, separating plaque formation from channel function. These assays do not establish the permeability of every physiological substrate or the function of N54K/Cx30 plaques in the cochlear-derived model.

evidence.snippet: The N54K mutant exhibits transdominant inhibition of endogenous Cx43 in REKs.
evidence.explanation: Transdominant effect on the endogenous keratinocyte connexin in rat epidermal keratinocytes.

evidence.snippet: Only cells expressing the N54K mutant exhibited a significant decrease in detectable dye transfer, suggesting that the N54K mutant had a modest transdominant-negative effect on endogenous Cx43
evidence.explanation: Functional effect in rat epidermal keratinocytes; plaque abundance itself was not reduced.

evidence.snippet: It is important to note that a transdominant interaction with a non-traditional binding partner, such as Cx43, should be considered a gain-of-function property
evidence.explanation: Authors distinguish acquisition of an abnormal interaction from its inhibitory effect on coupling.

steps/4.description: In HeLa cells, N54K increases intracellular wild-type Cx26 and Cx30 and reduces their dye coupling. In rat epidermal keratinocytes, intracellular Cx43 signal increases and dye transfer decreases modestly, without reducing Cx43 plaque number. An abnormal interaction with a non-traditional partner can be termed a gain of function while reducing the partner network's communication; these are compatible descriptions. Patient epidermal Cx30 upregulation is only a proposed compensation, not proof that this interaction occurs in vivo.

evidence.snippet: We found that only REKs expressing the N54K mutant had reduced dye transfer.
evidence.explanation: Direct keratinocyte dye-transfer result; downstream hyperkeratosis remains an inference.

steps/5.description: Reduced gap junction-mediated intercellular transport between epidermal keratinocytes, proposed as the proximate cause of the regional acral hyperkeratosis. The step from reduced coupling to hyperkeratosis is not characterized.

evidence.snippet: These approaches have provided evidence supporting a role of gap junctions and hemichannels in K(+) removal and recycling in the ear, as well as possible roles for nutrient passage, in the cochlea.
evidence.explanation: General connexin physiology of the cochlea; not BPS-specific.

evidence.snippet: GJB2 gene (that encodes Cx26) mutations are causal of hearing loss highlighting the importance of Cx26-based channel signaling amongst the supporting cells in the organ of Corti.
evidence.explanation: Places the relevant connexin 26 network in organ of Corti supporting cells.

steps/6.description: Disrupted connexin signaling among cochlear supporting cells is a proposed explanation for BPS hearing loss. General connexin studies support candidate roles in potassium buffering/recycling, nutrient transfer and intercellular signaling, without establishing which is causal for BPS. N54K trafficking was studied in immortalized HEI-OC1 cells, not mature supporting cells or patient cochlear tissue. Cx30 restored plaque localization there without a demonstrated N54K functional rescue. BPS-specific potassium dysregulation, oxidative injury and hair-cell death have not been demonstrated by these studies.

evidence.snippet: Bart-Pumphrey syndrome (BPS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by sensorineural hearing loss, palmoplantar keratoderma, knuckle pads, and leukonychia, which show considerable phenotypic variability.

evidence.snippet: Hearing loss and knuckle pads are the more commonly seen findings of this syndrome.

steps/7.description: Circumscribed hyperkeratotic thickenings over finger or toe joints, sometimes extending to the wrist. Onset may be in childhood. They can be mistaken for warts; one patient developed atrophic scars after cryotherapy for that misdiagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Bart-Pumphrey syndrome (BPS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by sensorineural hearing loss, palmoplantar keratoderma, knuckle pads, and leukonychia, which show considerable phenotypic variability.

evidence.snippet: Leukonychia totalis was present as the most common manifestation in all affected members while knuckle pads were only present in male members.

steps/9.description: Palmar and plantar thickening ranges from mild focal or punctate changes to diffuse or striate keratoderma. It may accentuate skin creases and may escape the patient's notice. Age-related worsening occurred in one clinically diagnosed family but was absent in another; progression is not uniform.

evidence.snippet: Bart-Pumphrey syndrome (BPS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by sensorineural hearing loss, palmoplantar keratoderma, knuckle pads, and leukonychia, which show considerable phenotypic variability.

Some relatives in another clinically diagnosed family had no detected hearing loss; the male-only pattern in that pedigree is not an established sex-specific inheritance rule.

evidence.snippet: BPDCN skin tumours first develop at sun-exposed anatomical sites and are distinguished by clonally expanded mutations induced by ultraviolet (UV) radiation
evidence.explanation: Establishes the exposure's fingerprint in the tumours themselves rather than by epidemiologic inference.

evidence.snippet: Overall, founder clones contained recurrent alterations in TET2 (5 out of 5 cases, 4 out of 5 cases with ≥2 alterations), ASXL1 (3 out of 5 cases) and splicing-factors (3 out of 5 cases), including ZRSR2 (2 out of 5 cases), suggesting privileged roles in premalignant evolution in BPDCN (Fig. 1e (top)).
evidence.explanation: Human phylogenies support recurrent founder lesions, without a fixed TET2-before-ASXL1 mutation order.

evidence.snippet: The number of cases is small, but the variant allele fraction (VAF) sums of the TET2 mutations, as well as the persistence of TET2 mutations in a case of relapsed BPDCN, suggest an ancestral/founder nature of TET2 clones in the cases.
evidence.explanation: The five-patient series infers ancestral and biallelic involvement from VAF and persistence rather than direct phasing.

steps/9.description: Somatic TET2 alterations occur in premalignant marrow hematopoietic precursors that can give rise to BPDCN. Truncating loss-of-function variants are common, but not every reported missense allele has demonstrated functional loss. Multiple TET2 variants and high combined variant allele fractions suggest biallelic involvement in some series; these observations do not phase every pair of variants. TET2 and ASXL1 can occur in different orders within branching clones.

evidence.snippet: Overall, founder clones contained recurrent alterations in TET2 (5 out of 5 cases, 4 out of 5 cases with ≥2 alterations), ASXL1 (3 out of 5 cases) and splicing-factors (3 out of 5 cases), including ZRSR2 (2 out of 5 cases), suggesting privileged roles in premalignant evolution in BPDCN (Fig. 1e (top)).
evidence.explanation: Human phylogenies support recurrent founder lesions, without a fixed TET2-before-ASXL1 mutation order.

evidence.snippet: All 3 ASXL1 mutations were the c.1934dupG (p.Gly646Trpfs*12) variant, with the VAFs ranging from 24% to 28%.
evidence.explanation: This specific frameshift recurred in the small series; the statement is cohort-bounded.

steps/10.description: Somatic truncating ASXL1 variants affect chromatin regulation and can occur in ancestral marrow clones shared with BPDCN. The c.1934dupG allele occurred in all three ASXL1-mutant cases in a small institutional series; this does not define every ASXL1 alteration in BPDCN.

evidence.snippet: Whole-exome sequencing data were also used for cytogenetic CNV analysis, which highlighted extensive losses along the chromosome 9 and the associated deletion of the tumor suppressor CDKN2A gene in 8 out of 14 BPDCN samples (57%) (Online Supplementary Figure S2), as already reported in the literature.12,15,20
evidence.explanation: Primary copy-number analysis directly supports chromosome-9 CDKN2A loss; the other tumor suppressors are on different chromosomes.

evidence.snippet: These included loss of 7p (which harbors IKZF1), 9p (CDKN2A, CDKN2B), 12p (CDKN1B, ETV6), 13q (RB1), and 17p (TP53; Supplementary Fig. S2).
evidence.explanation: Copy-number analysis of purified BPDCN cells places the recurrent losses on separate chromosomes.

steps/11.description: Recurrent copy-number loss at chromosome 9p21.3 removes CDKN2A/CDKN2B cell-cycle inhibitors. CDKN1B and RB1 can also be deleted in BPDCN, but they reside on chromosomes 12 and 13, respectively, and are separate lesions. Loss of CDKN2A can cooperate with MYB-driven cell-cycle deregulation.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that 8q24/MYC rearrangements occur in 10-15% of BPDCN, often partnered with non-immunoglobulin chromosomal loci, and may play a role in BPDCN pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: The primary series behind this node, giving both the frequency and the non-immunoglobulin partner pattern.

evidence.snippet: One-third of cases of BPDCN harbor the 8q24 rearrangement, most frequently with 6p21 harboring RUNX2, which is associated with immunoblastoid cytomorphology and MYC expression.
evidence.explanation: A higher frequency estimate from a cytogenetics review, plus the RUNX2 partner and the cytomorphologic association. Curated alongside the 10-15% figure rather than in place of it, because the two disagree.

steps/12.description: Rearrangement of the MYC locus, most often partnered with 6p21 (RUNX2) rather than an immunoglobulin locus, driving MYC overexpression. Reported frequencies differ substantially by cohort and ascertainment - 12% in one single-institution karyotype series, about a third in a cytogenetics review - and the rearranged cases are associated with an immunoblastoid cytomorphology.

evidence.snippet: Loss-of-function mutations in ZRSR2, an X chromosome gene encoding a splicing factor, are enriched in BPDCN, and nearly all mutations occur in males.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the recurrence of the lesion in BPDCN and its near-exclusive occurrence in males.

steps/13.description: Loss of the X-linked splicing factor ZRSR2 causes intron retention with a strong U12-intron bias, while also affecting selected U2 introns. Mutations were found in 24 of 93 BPDCN cases, 23 in males and one in a female; truncating loss-of-function variants occurred only in males in that cohort. ZRSR2 contributes to the male predominance but does not explain all of it.

evidence.snippet: revealed that IKZF1, a gene encoding a transcription factor required for the differentiation of plasmacytoid dendritic cell precursors, is focally inactivated through recurrent structural alterations in this neoplasm
evidence.explanation: Direct whole-genome evidence for recurrent focal IKZF1 inactivation and its role in pDC precursor differentiation.

steps/14.description: Recurrent deletions and unbalanced rearrangements disrupt IKZF1. Structural alterations were detected in 13 of 25 patients across the sequencing and extension cohorts; this count includes one focal duplication whose functional effect was inferred. Reduced IKZF1 activity is implicated in altered pDC differentiation and adhesion-gene expression. Patient expression signatures and comparisons with experimental IKZF1-deficient systems support this interpretation, without direct demonstration of skin homing.

evidence.snippet: Rearrangements of the hematopoietic transcription factor MYB are recurrently found in 20% of patients with blastic plasmacytoid DC neoplasm (BPDCN), a rare leukemia arising from cells of the plasmacytoid DC (pDC) lineage
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the recurrence of MYB rearrangement in BPDCN.

steps/15.description: BPDCN-associated MYB rearrangements retain the N-terminal DNA-binding domain and remove or alter C-terminal regulation. MYB::PLEKHO1 produces a chimeric protein, whereas the out-of-frame MYB::ZFAT rearrangement produces truncated MYB without a ZFAT protein segment. Engineered models support enhanced G2/M-gene binding and leukemogenic potential, with partner-dependent requirements for cooperating lesions.

evidence.snippet: Using RNAi screening, we identified the E-box transcription factor TCF4 as a master regulator of the BPDCN oncogenic program.
evidence.explanation: Identifies TCF4 as the master regulator this node is built on.

evidence.snippet: High-throughput drug screening revealed that bromodomain and extra-terminal domain inhibitors (BETis) induced BPDCN apoptosis, which was attributable to disruption of a BPDCN-specific transcriptional network controlled by TCF4-dependent super-enhancers.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the BRD4/super-enhancer component of the network and its pharmacological tractability.

steps/16.description: TCF4 maintains a BPDCN-specific transcriptional program involving BRD4-associated super-enhancers. TCF4 or BRD4 depletion and BET inhibition reduce survival in CAL1 and GEN2.2 cells; rescue experiments support the specificity of TCF4 knockdown. This maintenance dependency is distinct from proving how an ancestral clone first transforms.

evidence.snippet: MYB fusions found in patients with BPDCN increased the magnitude of DNA binding at these locations, and this was linked to BPDCN-associated gene expression changes.
evidence.explanation: Links the fusion's increased binding at G2/M loci to the expression changes this node names.

steps/17.description: MYB occupies and regulates G2/M cell-cycle genes in BPDCN with and without MYB fusions. Endogenous-locus MYB knock-ins in the K562 human leukemia line demonstrate stronger binding by truncated MYB and MYB::PLEKHO1 than by wild-type MYB. These experiments complement BPDCN-cell and xenograft chromatin profiles; K562 is not a BPDCN model.

evidence.snippet: we identify monoallelic deletion of NR3C1 (5q31), encoding the glucocorticoid receptor (GCR), in 13 of 47 (28%) BPDCN patients
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the recurrence of the monoallelic NR3C1 deletion this node describes.

evidence.snippet: Haploinsufficiency for NR3C1 defined a subset of BPDCN with lowered GCR expression and extremely poor overall survival (P = .0006).
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the reduced receptor expression and the prognostic consequence.

steps/18.description: Monoallelic NR3C1 deletion was detected in 13 of 47 BPDCN cases and associated with reduced glucocorticoid-receptor expression and poorer survival in the index cohort. GCR knockdown and a separately identified NR3C1 fusion support impaired glucocorticoid responses and altered chromatin regulation. The deletion does not imply an identical 50% expression reduction or clinically proven steroid failure in every affected patient.

evidence.snippet: Re-expression of full-length DPH1 also restored the cytotoxic activity of tagraxofusp in resistant cells
evidence.explanation: DPH1 add-back directly reversed acquired resistance in CAL1 BPDCN cells.

evidence.snippet: Expression of DPH1, encoding a diphthamide pathway enzyme, was reduced by DNA CpG methylation in resistant cells.
evidence.explanation: Primary study of acquired resistance; CAL1 and AML perturbation experiments establish methylation-associated downregulation.

steps/19.description: Acquired tagraxofusp resistance can involve reduced diphthamide-pathway activity, including methylation-associated DPH1 downregulation. DPH1 loss impairs the eEF2 substrate modification required for toxin-mediated ADP-ribosylation. CAL1 knockout/add-back and azacitidine experiments establish a reversible route; small patient and xenograft analyses support pathway impairment in vivo. CD123 was retained in this study, but this does not exclude other resistance mechanisms or antigen loss in other settings.

evidence.snippet: IRF7 intron 4 was aberrantly retained in ZRSR2-mutant BPDCN (2 of 2), and the same intron–exon region was also misspliced in SRSF2-mutated (4 of 4) and SF3B1-mutated (1 of 1) cases but not in splicing factor wild-type BPDCN or in normal pDCs (Supplementary Table S4).
evidence.explanation: IRF7 intron 4 is a weak, delayed-spliced U2-type intron; it is not a U12 intron.

evidence.snippet: Wild-type intronless IRF7, which would not require ZRSR2 for splicing, restored LPS-induced growth arrest in ZRSR2-mutant cells, whereas inactive IRF7 did not (Supplementary Fig. S5D).
evidence.explanation: Endogenous-locus intronless IRF7 rescue links the splicing defect to the impaired stimulated growth response.

steps/20.description: ZRSR2-mutant BPDCN retains the weak fourth intron of IRF7 and fails to increase IRF7 protein normally after TLR stimulation. IRF7 is not a U12-intron-containing transcript. Missplicing in SRSF2- and SF3B1-mutant cases indicates that this defect is not restricted to ZRSR2.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with our GEP experiments, western blot analyses revealed global loss of H3K27me3 under attenuated GCR signaling (Figure 3D; supplemental Figure 3D).
evidence.explanation: GCR knockdown or fusion expression in dexamethasone-treated CAL1 cells reduced H3K27me3; direct physical regulation of PRC2 remains unresolved.

steps/21.description: In dexamethasone-treated CAL1 cells, GCR knockdown or expression of the NR3C1 fusion reduces global H3K27me3 and repressive marks at HOXA promoters. The associated expression program resembles loss of EZH2 activity. The molecular connection between GCR and PRC2 remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: lincRNA-3q knockdown in CAL-1 and U937 cells induced a G1/S arrest (Figure 4Cand supplemental Figure 4C, respectively), without inducing cell death (supplemental Figure 4D).
evidence.explanation: CAL1 knockdown impairs cell-cycle progression; U937 is a separate AML comparator.

steps/22.description: The nuclear lincRNA-3q is aberrantly expressed in BPDCN samples. Its depletion in CAL1 reduces E2F-associated transcription, clonogenicity and G1/S progression without directly inducing cell death in the reported assay. This is a separate experimentally supported dependency; whether NR3C1 loss causes its activation is still proposed.

evidence.snippet: Overall, founder clones contained recurrent alterations in TET2 (5 out of 5 cases, 4 out of 5 cases with ≥2 alterations), ASXL1 (3 out of 5 cases) and splicing-factors (3 out of 5 cases), including ZRSR2 (2 out of 5 cases), suggesting privileged roles in premalignant evolution in BPDCN (Fig. 1e (top)).
evidence.explanation: Human phylogenies support recurrent founder lesions, without a fixed TET2-before-ASXL1 mutation order.

steps/23.description: Premalignant hematopoietic clones in the marrow can retain multilineage differentiation and share founder mutations with BPDCN skin tumors or another myeloid neoplasm. Additional lineage-specific alterations accompany transformation. Shared variants establish ancestry but do not by themselves prove that an overt myeloid cancer directly converted into BPDCN.

evidence.snippet: functional analyses coupled with gene expression profiling identified corticoresistance and loss-of-EZH2 function as major downstream consequences of NR3C1 deletion in BPDCN
evidence.explanation: Names corticoresistance as a demonstrated downstream consequence of the NR3C1 lesion, which is what this node records.

steps/24.description: Attenuated glucocorticoid-receptor function reduces glucocorticoid-induced responses in CAL1 perturbation experiments. This provides a potential resistance mechanism relevant to steroid-containing regimens, rather than a validated treatment-selection rule for all NR3C1-deleted patients.

evidence.snippet: expression of MYB fusions in vivo impaired DC differentiation and induced transformation to generate a mouse model of myeloid-dendritic acute leukemia.
evidence.explanation: In vivo demonstration that a BPDCN driver lesion produces a dendritic-cell differentiation block coupled to transformation.

evidence.snippet: characterized by neoplastic cells that are positive for CD123, CD4, BDCA2, and TCL1 and aberrant expression of CD56
evidence.explanation: Human evidence for the retained pDC identity markers this node asserts, so the node does not rest on model-organism evidence alone.

steps/25.description: Malignant cells retain a pDC-associated immunophenotype while showing abnormal differentiation and function. MYB perturbation models directly impair dendritic differentiation; IKZF1-related changes provide another proposed route. These findings do not establish a single developmental arrest point in every BPDCN.

evidence.snippet: Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic-cell neoplasm (BPDCN) is an aggressive hematologic cancer that is caused by transformed plasmacytoid dendritic cells that overexpress interleukin-3 receptor subunit alpha (IL3RA or CD123).
evidence.explanation: States CD123 overexpression on the transformed pDCs as the defining molecular feature of this node.

steps/26.description: BPDCN blasts commonly express high levels of CD123, the IL3RA subunit. This provides the binding target for tagraxofusp, pivekimab and investigational CD123-directed cellular therapies. Tagraxofusp delivers a diphtheria toxin payload; receptor expression alone does not establish that IL-3 signaling drives BPDCN. Earlier RNAi screens suggest an IL3RA dependency, but other treatment targets include BCL2 and transcriptional regulators.

evidence.snippet: We found that primary BPDCN cells were dependent on the antiapoptotic protein BCL2 and were uniformly sensitive to the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax, as measured by direct cytotoxicity, apoptosis assays, and dynamic BH3 profiling.
evidence.explanation: Functional profiling establishes BCL2 dependence in the tested primary samples; it does not guarantee response in every patient.

steps/27.description: BH3 profiling demonstrated BCL2 dependence in the tested primary BPDCN samples, supported by venetoclax-induced apoptosis and responses in patient-derived xenografts. This functional dependence provides a therapeutic rationale but does not guarantee a durable clinical response in every patient. It is separate from the activation-coupled apoptosis defect associated with ZRSR2.

evidence.snippet: After UV exposure (100, 500 μJ cm−2), Tet2 knockout caused a further increase in the proportion of surviving pDCs, but had no protective effect on cDCs (Fig. 5e).
evidence.explanation: Tet2 knockout was tested in differentiated mouse HOXB8 cultures ex vivo, not by inducing skin tumors with UV in living mice.

evidence.snippet: A reconstruction of tumour phylogenies reveals that UV damage can precede the acquisition of alterations associated with malignant transformation
evidence.explanation: Supports the ordering claim - UV damage before transformation - that makes this a selective step rather than a consequence of the tumour.

steps/28.description: Human tumor phylogenies identify a UV-associated route in which premalignant pDC-lineage cells acquire UV damage in skin before or during transformation. In an ex vivo mouse HOXB8 differentiation system, Tet2 knockout selectively protects pDCs from UV-induced death. Together these findings support selection in sun-exposed skin in some cases, without making UV exposure necessary for every BPDCN or demonstrating complete UV-driven transformation in vivo.

evidence.snippet: up-regulation of cellular processes responsible for cell-cell and cell-ECM interactions, which is a hallmark of IKZF1 deficiency, was prominent in BPDCN
evidence.explanation: Reports the adhesion-program upregulation and attributes it to IKZF1 deficiency.

steps/29.description: Patient BPDCN transcriptomes show increased cell-cell and extracellular-matrix interaction programs. Comparisons with IKZF1-deficient experimental systems implicate IKZF1 dysfunction. A contribution to skin homing is plausible but has not been established by BPDCN migration or homing rescue experiments.

evidence.snippet: IRF7 and TRAIL induction by LPS were partially rescued in ZRSR2-mutant cells by overexpression of wild-type ZRSR2 (Fig. 6E).
evidence.explanation: The CAL1 rescue experiment supports impaired IRF7-dependent activation and TRAIL induction downstream of ZRSR2 loss.

steps/30.description: After inflammatory TLR stimulation, ZRSR2-deficient pDC-lineage cells show reduced induction of IRF7, type I interferons and the proapoptotic mediator TRAIL. This is a selective impairment: other secreted mediators and downstream responses to exogenous TRAIL remain intact.

evidence.snippet: Knockout of ZRSR2 conferred relative protection from LPS- or R848-induced apoptosis (Fig. 6B). The growth rate of CAL1 cells at steady state was not changed by ZRSR2 mutation.
evidence.explanation: CAL1 perturbation demonstrates a stimulation-dependent survival advantage.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with exogenous TRAIL promoted apoptosis equivalently in control and ZRSR2-mutant CAL1 cells, as well as in normal pDCs and BPDCN, demonstrating that the cell death response downstream of TRAIL was intact (Fig. 6D; Supplementary Fig. S4B).
evidence.explanation: The defect concerns activation-coupled apoptosis rather than an inability to execute cell death.

evidence.snippet: Wild-type intronless IRF7, which would not require ZRSR2 for splicing, restored LPS-induced growth arrest in ZRSR2-mutant cells, whereas inactive IRF7 did not (Supplementary Fig. S5D).
evidence.explanation: Endogenous-locus intronless IRF7 rescue links the splicing defect to the impaired stimulated growth response.

steps/31.description: ZRSR2-deficient cells are relatively protected from growth arrest and apoptosis after TLR stimulation because activation and TRAIL induction are impaired. The advantage is stimulus-dependent; ZRSR2 loss did not increase baseline CAL1 growth, and exogenous TRAIL can still trigger apoptosis.

evidence.snippet: Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) is an aggressive hematologic malignancy that presents with skin nodules and tumors, lymph node and splenic enlargement, central nervous system involvement, circulating leukemia, and/or bone marrow infiltration
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the compartments the expanded clone reaches, which are this node's downstream targets.

steps/32.description: The differentiation-arrested, apoptosis-resistant clone expands, and this expanded population is what subsequently distributes to skin, marrow, blood, lymph nodes and the leptomeninges.

evidence.snippet: Integrating transcriptional data with T-cell receptor sequencing via shared barcodes reveals significant T-cell exhaustion in BPDCN that is positively correlated with T-cell clonotype expansion.
evidence.explanation: Direct single-cell evidence for the T-cell exhaustion this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: T-cells in BPDCN patients consistently upregulate interferon alpha (IFNA) response and downregulate tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFA) pathways
evidence.explanation: Supports the specific pathway directions described in this node.

steps/33.description: Single-cell profiling of five BPDCN marrows and five healthy controls found increased interferon-alpha response signatures, reduced TNF-alpha signaling signatures and higher CD8 memory T-cell exhaustion scores. TCR analysis in four evaluable patients linked larger clonotypes to higher exhaustion scores. These are transcriptional associations; chronic interferon secretion by accumulated tumor cells was proposed but not directly measured as the cause.

evidence.explanation: Direct examination documented cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy.

evidence.snippet: Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) scans showed lymphadenopathy at the base of the neck, mediastinum, axilla, and bilateral inguinal regions, splenomegaly, and mild pleural effusion (Fig. S1E).
evidence.explanation: Direct imaging in the BPDCN index patient documents splenic enlargement.

steps/34.description: BPDCN cells infiltrate lymph nodes and spleen. Lymph node enlargement and splenomegaly are clinical manifestations, while registry primary-site proportions describe a different measure of disease distribution.

evidence.explanation: Direct BPDCN skin histology documents dermal-to-subcutaneous extension and monomorphic cells.

evidence.snippet: The appearance of the disease in the skin biopsy consists of a typical monomorphic and diffuse infiltrate involving the dermis, with sparing of the epidermis and the presence of a visible Grenz zone.
evidence.explanation: The review describes the characteristic architecture, which is not sufficient alone for diagnosis.

steps/35.description: Blasts infiltrate the dermis and may extend into subcutaneous fat, producing erythematous to violaceous plaques or nodules. Skin disease may precede systemic involvement, coexist with it, or be absent at presentation.

evidence.snippet: BPDCN arises from plasmacytoid dendritic cells, manifesting primarily in the skin, bone marrow, and lymph nodes, occasionally involving the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence.explanation: Names marrow as a primary compartment of involvement.

steps/36.description: BPDCN cells may infiltrate marrow and circulate in blood. Marrow disease can occur at presentation or during progression and does not invariably follow cutaneous disease.

evidence.snippet: This presents challenges in diagnosis and treatment, with CNS involvement often overlooked in standard diagnostic workups due to BPDCN's rarity and patients often being neurologically asymptomatic at diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: States that CNS involvement is present but clinically silent and therefore under-detected.

evidence.snippet: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples positive for tumor plasmacytoid dendritic cells were found in 6/10 (60%) cases studied at diagnosis
evidence.explanation: Flow cytometry detected occult CSF disease in six of ten newly diagnosed patients in a small prospective cohort; this is not a population prevalence.

steps/37.description: BPDCN blasts may infiltrate the leptomeningeal/CSF compartment while neurologic examination remains normal. CNS involvement is also a recognized relapse pattern. Sensitive CSF flow cytometry can detect occult disease; the small available cohorts do not define a uniform prevalence at diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: The most common findings in the peripheral blood are thrombocytopenia (78%), anemia (65%), and neutropenia (34%).
evidence.explanation: The review records disease-associated cytopenias; it does not establish marrow replacement as the cause in every patient.

evidence.snippet: His platelets had been persistently below 10,000/μL despite transfusion, predating venetoclax treatment and likely related to bone marrow infiltration by BPDCN.
evidence.explanation: A BPDCN patient had severe thrombocytopenia before venetoclax; marrow infiltration was the authors' likely explanation.

steps/38.description: Marrow infiltration can impair normal hematopoiesis and contribute to cytopenias. Anemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia are reported manifestations, but an individual cytopenia requires assessment of other causes and treatment effects.

evidence.snippet: characterized by disseminated, erythematous or bluish-livid plaques or nodi
evidence.explanation: Describes the lesion morphology and distribution this phenotype names.

evidence.snippet: tumor formation in the skin (in ∼90% of cases)
evidence.explanation: Introductory literature summary estimates skin tumors in approximately 90% of cases; this is not a newly measured cohort proportion.

steps/39.description: Disseminated erythematous to bluish-livid, often bruise-like plaques and nodules, the presenting feature in the large majority of patients.

steps/4.description: Campylobacter adhesins bind fibronectin on polarized epithelial cells, triggering host signaling needed for invasion.

steps/8.description: Host inflammatory responses and epithelial lesions produce fluid/blood loss and symptomatic enteritis.

steps/9.description: Some patients develop delayed extraintestinal immune-mediated complications after acute Campylobacter infection.

evidence.snippet: A novel mutation of an essential splice site in the C19orf70 gene encoding QIL1 induces severe mitochondrial encephalopathy, hepatopathy and lactate acidosis consistent with psychomotor retardation.
evidence.explanation: The German allele and the syndrome it produced.

evidence.snippet: whole-exome sequencing of a patient presenting with hepato-encephalopathy and MTDPS identified a novel homozygous frameshift variant, c.13_29del (p.Trp6Profs*71) in MICOS13
evidence.explanation: The Japanese allele, in an unrelated patient.

evidence.snippet: Using homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing the patients were found to be homozygous for the p.(Gly15Glufs*75) variant in the QIL1/MIC13 (C19orf70) gene.
evidence.explanation: The founding allele and the report that first established this gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: The variant introduces a premature termination codon, leading to a truncated protein that lacks the second RDSWN motif, which is critical for MIC13 function.
evidence.explanation: A fourth allele, and the one report that identifies which part of the protein the truncation removes rather than only that it truncates.

steps/1.description:
Several reported alleles, all loss of function and all removing the protein rather than altering it. The gene is small and every reported variant truncates it.
The founding allele is the homozygous frameshift p.(Gly15Glufs*75), in a consanguineous brother and sister. Later reports add a splice-site variant in C19orf70, the homozygous frameshift c.13_29del (p.Trp6Profs*71) which truncates within the first ten residues, and c.209dupT (p.Ala73Argfs*32), which removes the second RDSWN motif required for MIC13 function.
Fibroblasts from the c.13_29del patient have no detectable MICOS13, so these are true nulls rather than hypomorphs.

evidence.snippet: Disassembly of MICOS complex subunits displays lack of MIC10-MIC26-MIC27-QIL1 subcomplex, resulting in aberrant cristae structure and a loss of cristae junctions and contact sites.
evidence.explanation: Names the specific subcomplex that is lost, which is the precise form of the assembly claim and is what distinguishes it from a general statement that MICOS is disrupted.

evidence.snippet: We found loss of MICOS13 protein and fewer cristae structures in the mitochondria of fibroblasts derived from the patient.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation in a second patient's cells, and the direct demonstration that the protein itself is absent.

evidence.snippet: In patient fibroblasts both MICOS subunits QIL1/MIC13 and MIC10 were absent whereas MIC60 was present in a comparable abundance to that of the control.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the assembly failure is selective: one MICOS arm collapses while the MIC60 core is retained. The preserved MIC60 is what makes this a partial complex rather than an absent one.

evidence.snippet: QIL1 absence in patients' fibroblasts was associated with MICOS disassembly, abnormal cristae, mild cytochrome c oxidase defect, and sensitivity to glucose withdrawal.
evidence.explanation: A second sibling pair, reported by a different group in the same year, in which the same assembly failure and the same cristae abnormality were found. This is independent replication of the node rather than a further description of the founding family.

evidence.snippet: MICOS assembly and cristae morphology were not efficiently rescued by over-expression of other MICOS subunits in patient fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: The specificity control the other patient reports lack. The assembly failure is not a generic shortage of MICOS subunits that any other subunit can make up for, so MICOS13 is required in its own right rather than as one of several interchangeable components.

evidence.snippet: MIC13 acts as a critical bridge between two MICOS subcomplexes. Deletion of MIC13 causes loss of CJs resulting in cristae accumulating as concentric rings and specific destabilization of the MIC10-subcomplex.
evidence.explanation: States the bridging function that explains why one arm of the complex collapses while the MIC60 core is retained, and confirms the selectivity of the MIC10-subcomplex loss in an experimental system rather than in patient material.

steps/2.description:
MICOS13 is a small subunit whose job is to build and hold together the rest of the complex. Its loss is therefore not the loss of one component among seven: a defined subcomplex comprising MIC10, MIC26, MIC27 and QIL1 fails to form.
In Kishita et al.'s patient the protein was directly shown to be absent from fibroblast mitochondria, so the assembly failure follows from protein loss rather than from a hypomorphic variant with residual function.
The founding report makes the selectivity sharper still. In those patients' fibroblasts both MIC13 and MIC10 were absent while MIC60 was present at normal abundance. MIC60 is the core of the other MICOS subcomplex, so what fails is one arm of the complex rather than the complex as a whole - which is a more specific claim than "MICOS is disrupted" and is consistent with the MIC10-MIC26-MIC27-QIL1 subcomplex loss reported independently.

evidence.snippet: resulting in aberrant cristae structure and a loss of cristae junctions and contact sites.
evidence.explanation: States the structural lesion directly.

evidence.snippet: disturbed hepatocellular function with abnormal cristae morphology in liver and cerebellar and vermis atrophy
evidence.explanation: Abnormal cristae morphology in patient liver. This is the one place the architectural lesion is documented in an affected human organ rather than inferred from fibroblasts, which is why it is graded HUMAN_CLINICAL.

steps/3.description:
The structural lesion of the disease. Cristae junctions are the narrow necks that connect each crista to the inner boundary membrane, and they do two things: they hold the folded surface area on which respiratory complexes are concentrated, and they partition the intermembrane space so that the crista lumen is a distinct compartment. Contact sites link the inner membrane to the outer.
Losing them is therefore not simply a morphological finding. It removes the geometry that makes oxidative phosphorylation efficient, which is why an architectural defect presents as a bioenergetic disease.

evidence.snippet: In liver and muscle tissue, the activity of the respiratory chain complexes (OXPHOS) was severely impaired.
evidence.explanation: The biochemical deficiency in patient tissue, in the two organs the disease affects.

evidence.snippet: Stable expression of a wild-type MICOS13 cDNA in the patients fibroblasts using a lentivirus system rescued mitochondrial respiratory chain complex deficiencies.
evidence.explanation: The rescue experiment. This is the strongest single piece of evidence in the entry: it establishes that the respiratory deficiency is caused by the absence of MICOS13 rather than merely correlated with it.

steps/4.description:
Multiple OXPHOS complexes are deficient at once, in liver and muscle. "Combined" is the diagnostic label and it is also the mechanistic clue: a defect in one complex's subunits or assembly factors affects that complex, whereas a defect in the membrane they all occupy affects all of them.
The strongest evidence that this is secondary to the architectural lesion rather than an independent problem is a rescue: expressing wild-type MICOS13 in the patient's own fibroblasts restored respiratory chain function.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that the novel c.13_29del (p.Trp6Profs*71) MICOS13 variant causes hepato-encephalopathy with MTDPS. We propose that MICOS13 is classified as the cause of MTDPS.
evidence.explanation: The depletion finding and the classification proposal, quoted with the authors' own hedging ("suggest", "propose") preserved.

evidence.snippet: Most MTDPS is caused by mutations in genes that disrupt deoxyribonucleotide metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that MICOS13 does not belong to the usual mechanistic class of depletion genes, which is why the finding is recorded as an open question rather than as a settled mechanism. INDIRECT because it is background about the disease group, not an observation in this patient.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, analysis of mitochondrial DNA copy number revealed a mitochondrial depletion in the patient.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of the depletion finding in an unrelated patient, which is what raises it above a single-report observation.

evidence.snippet: It was more frequently seen in ATPase related disorders, with mitochondrial DNA depletion or deletion, but not in patients with single respiratory chain complex deficiencies.
evidence.explanation: Connects the two findings that co-occur in these patients: across 977 patients, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria tracks with mtDNA depletion and specifically not with isolated respiratory chain complex defects. INDIRECT because it is an association across a large mixed cohort, not an observation in a MICOS13 patient - but it is the reason the depletion and the aciduria are treated here as parts of one picture rather than as coincidence.

steps/5.description:
Reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number, found in Kishita et al.'s patient - the reason that group proposed reclassifying MICOS13 as a cause of mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome - and independently again in Ammar et al.'s patient six years later.
Two independent reports is what moves this from a single-patient observation towards a feature of the disease. It remains true that not every report measured copy number, so the denominator is the number who looked rather than the number who have it.
This is unusual for the gene class. Depletion syndromes are typically caused by defects in deoxyribonucleotide metabolism or in the mtDNA replication machinery, and MICOS13 is neither. The authors say so themselves. Whether cristae collapse causes depletion, or the two are parallel consequences of a failing organelle, is not established.

evidence.snippet: induces severe mitochondrial encephalopathy, hepatopathy and lactate acidosis consistent with psychomotor retardation
evidence.explanation: The clinical syndrome.

steps/6.description: The clinical endpoint: a severe infantile encephalopathy with liver disease and lactic acidosis. Fatal in the first reported patient.

edges/1.description: MICOS13 is required to assemble the complex, so losing it prevents assembly.

edges/2.description: The subcomplex that fails to form is the one that shapes cristae junctions.

edges/3.description: The complexes are intact but the membrane they work in is not.

edges/4.description: Reported in two patients, by two independent groups. Typed with unknown intermediates because no mechanism connecting cristae architecture to mtDNA copy number has been demonstrated here, and because the other three reports did not measure copy number at all.

edges/5.description: Impaired ATP production in the two most oxidative organs, with lactate accumulating as glycolysis substitutes.

evidence.snippet: MICOS13 (also known as QIL1, MIC13, or C19orf70) is a component of the MICOS complex, which plays crucial roles in the maintenance of cristae junctions at the mitochondrial inner membrane.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gene's identity across its four names and its function, in one sentence.

evidence.snippet: Given that the encoded putative protein contains only 9 residues from QIL1 and lacks the transmembrane domain primarily derived from exon 2, we conclude that the encoded protein corresponds to a functionally null allele
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that a splice-donor variant, not only a frameshift, produces a null allele here, which is what lets the entry treat the disease as loss of function regardless of variant class.

genes/0.notes:
MICOS13 goes by four names in the literature - MICOS13, QIL1, MIC13 and C19orf70 - and all four appear across the primary papers, sometimes in the same sentence. A literature search on any single one of them misses part of the evidence base; this was a practical problem in curating the entry and is worth knowing for anyone extending it.
The reported alleles are frameshift, splice-donor and duplication variants, and all are predicted or shown to be null. Guarani et al.'s c.30-1G>A is the clearest case: it removes the transmembrane-domain exon, so the predicted protein retains nine residues of MICOS13 and nothing else.
The gene encodes a small subunit of the MICOS complex whose function is assembly. Its loss removes a defined MIC10-MIC26-MIC27-QIL1 subcomplex rather than degrading MICOS uniformly.

treatments/0.description:
There is no disease-modifying treatment. Management is the general mitochondrial supportive approach: managing lactic acidosis, hepatic support, and developmental care.
The lentiviral rescue in patient fibroblasts shows the defect is correctable in principle, which is a statement about biology and not about therapy - it was done in the wrong tissue, at an unlimited time point, with a vector that has no route to brain or liver in a patient.

treatments/1.description: Autosomal recessive, 25% recurrence risk per pregnancy for carrier couples. The first reported patient died, so counselling here is often after a bereavement and includes prenatal testing options.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The published patients were classified differently, and the difference tracks what each group measured rather than any reported difference between the patients. The German report characterised respiratory chain activity in liver and muscle and did not report mtDNA copy number. The Japanese report found depletion and proposed MICOS13 be reclassified; Ammar et al. found it independently six years later. The disease's MONDO and OMIM identity is the COXPD one, which is why this entry sits under that name.
Two independent findings of depletion make it harder to dismiss as one patient's idiosyncrasy. And there is now a thread connecting it to the rest of the phenotype: in a 977-patient series, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria - which these patients also have - tracked with mtDNA depletion and specifically not with isolated respiratory chain deficiencies. So the two unexplained findings in this disease co-occur elsewhere too, which suggests a shared upstream cause in inner-membrane architecture rather than two coincidences.
The mechanistic question underneath is the interesting one. Depletion syndromes are diseases of nucleotide supply or of the replication machinery, and MICOS13 is a structural assembly factor - the second report's own introduction says so. So either cristae architecture influences mtDNA maintenance by a route nobody has described, or depletion is a parallel consequence of a failing organelle rather than a consequence of the cristae lesion. The causal edge to the depletion node in this entry is typed INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES for exactly this reason.
It is answerable cheaply: measure mtDNA copy number in the first patient's stored tissue, or in any future patient, and the question of whether depletion is a consistent feature stops depending on which assay someone happened to run.

evidence.snippet: All mutations cluster within the GTPase or middle domains, and structural modeling and existing functional data suggest a dominant-negative effect on DMN1 function.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the GTPase/middle-domain clustering and dominant-negative mechanism of DNM1 variants.

evidence.snippet: Seven patients (33.3%) carried the recurrent p.Arg237Trp mutation.
evidence.explanation: Documents the recurrent p.Arg237Trp variant as the most common DNM1 allele.

steps/0.description: De novo missense variants in DNM1 cluster in the GTPase and middle domains of dynamin-1 and act by a dominant-negative mechanism: mutant subunits incorporate into the dynamin oligomer that assembles around the neck of an endocytosing vesicle and poison its GTP-dependent fission activity. The recurrent p.Arg237Trp variant accounts for about one-third of cases.

evidence.snippet: The focal point of the vesicle cycle is Ca2+-triggered exocytosis that is followed by different routes of endocytosis and recycling.
evidence.explanation: Establishes endocytosis/recycling as the vesicle-cycle arm mediated by dynamin-1 and disrupted in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: We bring statistical evidence that mutations in DNM1 cause epileptic encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Establishes DNM1 (dynamin-1) loss as a cause of epileptic encephalopathy via disrupted synaptic transmission.

steps/1.description: Dynamin-1 is the fission GTPase that pinches off endocytosing synaptic vesicles from the presynaptic plasma membrane to regenerate the recycling vesicle pool. Dominant-negative impairment of dynamin-1 slows vesicle fission and retrieval, depleting release-ready vesicles during sustained neuronal firing and causing activity-dependent synaptic transmission failure — the "vesicle fission" disease.

evidence.snippet: A common phenotype emerged that included severe to profound intellectual disability and muscular hypotonia in all patients and an epilepsy characterized by infantile spasms in 16 of 21 patients, frequently evolving into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Documents the epilepsy (infantile spasms evolving to Lennox-Gastaut) and the severe neurodevelopmental impairment produced by the disorder.

steps/2.description: Activity-dependent failure of vesicle recycling disturbs the balance of cortical synaptic transmission, producing neuronal hyperexcitability and a severe early-onset epilepsy that characteristically begins with infantile spasms and often evolves into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, alongside impaired activity-dependent neurodevelopment.

evidence.snippet: an epilepsy characterized by infantile spasms in 16 of 21 patients, frequently evolving into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies infantile spasms as the characteristic seizure onset in DNM1 encephalopathy.

steps/3.description: Early-onset epilepsy that typically begins with infantile spasms and frequently evolves into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

evidence.snippet: A common phenotype emerged that included severe to profound intellectual disability and muscular hypotonia in all patients
evidence.explanation: Documents universal severe-to-profound intellectual disability.

steps/4.description: Severe to profound intellectual disability is present in all patients.

evidence.snippet: All mutations cluster within the GTPase or middle domains, and structural modeling and existing functional data suggest a dominant-negative effect on DMN1 function.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the domain clustering and dominant-negative mechanism of DNM1 variants.

evidence.snippet: We bring statistical evidence that mutations in DNM1 cause epileptic encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Independent statistical evidence that DNM1 variants cause epileptic encephalopathy.

genes/0.notes: De novo missense variants clustering in the GTPase and middle domains act by a dominant-negative mechanism. The recurrent p.Arg237Trp variant is among the most common recurrent variants in the epileptic encephalopathies.

evidence.snippet: Seizure outcome was assessed in 18 patients: 15 of 18 patients (83%) had refractory seizures. Three patients (17%) became seizure-free on treatment.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the incomplete response to antiseizure medication in the largest phenotyped DNM1 cohort.

evidence.snippet: Improvement in seizure control, but not seizure freedom, was observed with clobazam or clonazepam in 5 of 20 patients (25%), steroids or adrenocorticotropic hormone in 4 of 20 patients (20%), topiramate or zonisamide in 3 of 20 patients (15%), and the KD in 5 of 20 patients (25%).
evidence.explanation: Ranks the agents by reported benefit; the two benzodiazepines named first are the ones bound as therapeutic_agent here.

evidence.snippet: Worsening of seizures was reported in individual patients with levetiracetam, the KD, and cannabidiol.
evidence.explanation: Records the agents reported to aggravate seizures in individual patients. The same cohort reports sustained seizure freedom on levetiracetam with lamotrigine in another patient, so the effect is patient-specific rather than a property of the drug.

evidence.snippet: Seizures in patient 1 were refractory until the age of 6 years, when she became seizure-free on levetiracetam and lamotrigine.
evidence.explanation: The cohort's second durable seizure-free outcome, on levetiracetam with lamotrigine - the counterpart to the same drug worsening seizures in other patients.

treatments/0.description: Seizures, including infantile spasms and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, are managed with antiseizure medications and spasm-directed therapies; response is often incomplete. About 83% of patients remain refractory. Benzodiazepines (clobazam, clonazepam) are the agents most often reported to improve seizure control without producing seizure freedom, followed by steroids or ACTH and by topiramate or zonisamide. Levetiracetam and cannabidiol have each been reported to worsen seizures in individual patients, though levetiracetam combined with lamotrigine also produced sustained seizure freedom in another, so the effect is patient-specific rather than a property of the drug. No agent corrects the underlying dynamin-1 fission defect.

evidence.snippet: Patient 19 became seizure-free on the ketogenic diet (KD) at the age of 3.5 years; patient 21 had a dramatic reduction of myoclonic seizures in the second year of life while on the KD and continues to have frequent nonepileptic myoclonic jerks.
evidence.explanation: Records the two ketogenic-diet responders: one of the cohort's three seizure-free patients, and one with a dramatic reduction in myoclonic seizures rather than seizure freedom.

evidence.snippet: While the KD and treatment with benzodiazepines provided benefit in some patients, most patients had intractable epilepsy that continued into adulthood.
evidence.explanation: States the limit of the benefit directly: helpful in some patients, but the epilepsy stays intractable for the majority.

treatments/1.description: Ketogenic diet therapy is one of the few interventions reported to produce seizure freedom in DNM1 encephalopathy, and improved seizure control in about a quarter of patients. It is not uniformly beneficial - worsening has also been reported.

evidence.snippet: A common phenotype emerged that included severe to profound intellectual disability and muscular hypotonia in all patients
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the two impairments this supportive care targets - profound developmental impairment and hypotonia - are present in every patient, so the need is universal rather than occasional.

treatments/2.description: Multidisciplinary supportive care, including developmental therapies and management of hypotonia and feeding, is the mainstay.

evidence.snippet: All mutations were confirmed to be de novo, except for the affected sibling pair whose father was shown to have 5.5% mosaicism on leucocyte DNA.
evidence.explanation: Documents both halves of the counseling message: variants are almost always de novo, and the one exception was low-level parental mosaicism with sibling recurrence.

treatments/3.description: Genetic counseling addresses the de novo dominant mechanism, generally low recurrence risk, and the rare possibility of parental mosaicism.

evidence.snippet: All mutations cluster within the GTPase or middle domains, and structural modeling and existing functional data suggest a dominant-negative effect on DMN1 function.
evidence.explanation: Frames the dominant-negative inference as based on structural modeling and limited functional data, motivating deeper mechanistic confirmation.

evidence.snippet: Mutant DNM1a does not efficiently self-assemble into higher order complexes known to be necessary for proper dynamin function, and it also interferes with endocytic recycling in cell culture.
evidence.explanation: Provides cell-culture functional support for a dominant-negative (oligomer-assembly-poisoning) mechanism, though for a mouse Dnm1a variant rather than a human DEE allele.

open_questions/0.rationale: Most DNM1-DEE variants cluster in the GTPase and middle/stalk domains and are inferred to poison the wild-type dynamin oligomer rather than merely halve dosage, and mutant DNM1a fails to self-assemble and interferes with endocytic recycling in cell culture. The mechanistic distinction is therapeutically decisive: a true dominant-negative allele predicts benefit from allele-selective mutant knockdown (leaving the wild-type allele intact), whereas haploinsufficiency would call for gene supplementation. The strength of the dominant-negative inference — currently structural modeling plus limited functional data — and its variant-by-variant generality remain open.

evidence.snippet: In mice, the mutation results in defective synaptic transmission characterized by a slower recovery from depression after trains of stimulation.
evidence.explanation: Documents the activity-dependent nature of the synaptic defect (impaired recovery after high-frequency trains), the basis for the selective vulnerability hypothesis.

open_questions/1.rationale: Dynamin-1 acts in the recycling (endocytic) arm of the synaptic vesicle cycle, yet the disease manifests as a release/excitability disorder. A parsimonious reconciliation is that impaired fission slows vesicle retrieval only under sustained high-frequency activity, so neurons that fire fastest — parvalbumin-positive inhibitory interneurons — deplete their release-ready pool first, disinhibiting cortex and generating seizures. The fitful mouse shows exactly this activity-dependent signature (slower recovery from depression after stimulus trains), but whether interneuron-selective vulnerability is the causal driver of human hyperexcitability is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Fitful is a missense mutation in an exon that defines the DNM1a isoform, leaving intact the alternatively spliced exon that encodes DNM1b.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the mouse model is isoform-restricted (DNM1a only), unlike shared-domain human DEE variants, a key fidelity caveat.

evidence.snippet: The expression of the corresponding alternate transcripts is developmentally regulated, with DNM1b expression highest during early neuronal development and DNM1a expression increasing postnatally with synaptic maturation.
evidence.explanation: Documents the developmental DNM1a/DNM1b switch that may cause the isoform-restricted model to engage a different developmental window than human DNM1-DEE.

open_questions/2.rationale: The fitful mouse reproduces recurrent seizures and an activity-dependent synaptic defect, making it the primary in vivo DNM1 epilepsy model. But its fidelity to human DNM1-DEE is uncertain on two counts: fitful mutates only the DNM1a-defining exon while sparing DNM1b, whereas most human DEE variants sit in shared GTPase/middle domains affecting both isoforms; and DNM1b is highest in early development with DNM1a rising postnatally, so an isoform-restricted allele may engage a different developmental window than the human disease. Whether the mouse recapitulates the specific human trajectory (infantile spasms to Lennox-Gastaut, profound intellectual disability) rather than seizures in general is the open translational question.

evidence.snippet: Autophagy is a lysosome-based degradative process used to recycle obsolete cellular constituents and eliminate damaged organelles and aggregate-prone proteins. Their postmitotic nature and extremely polarized morphologies make neurons particularly vulnerable to disruptions caused by autophagy-lysosomal defects, especially as the brain ages.
evidence.explanation: This establishes that autophagy-lysosome dysfunction is a fundamental mechanism in neurodegenerative diseases including Parkinson disease and related Lewy body disorders.

evidence.snippet: In particular, we highlight antibody-based therapies to attenuate protein aggregation, compounds that enhance the generation of cellular energy and autophagy-enhancing agents as particular areas of promise.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that autophagy dysfunction is a key therapeutic target in DLB, with autophagy-enhancing agents being developed as potential disease-modifying therapies.

steps/0.description: Impaired autophagy and lysosomal functions are central to DLB pathogenesis. Neurons are particularly vulnerable to autophagy-lysosomal defects due to their postmitotic nature and polarized morphologies. Mutations in genes regulating autophagy and lysosomal functions, particularly GBA, contribute to impaired clearance of alpha-synuclein aggregates and damaged organelles. This dysfunction creates a vicious cycle where accumulating protein aggregates further impair the autophagic-lysosomal system.

evidence.snippet: Both are characterized morphologically by widespread cortical and subcortical α-synuclein/Lewy body plus β-amyloid and tau pathologies.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that alpha-synuclein aggregation forming Lewy bodies is the central pathological feature of DLB, distributed throughout cortical and subcortical regions.

steps/1.description: DLB is characterized morphologically by widespread cortical and subcortical alpha-synuclein aggregation forming Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites. The alpha-synuclein pathology leads to neuronal dysfunction and is central to the disease pathogenesis. The distribution and severity of Lewy body pathology correlates with cognitive impairment and clinical features.

evidence.snippet: Intravitam PET and post-mortem studies revealed more pronounced cortical atrophy, elevated cortical and limbic Lewy pathologies.
evidence.explanation: This demonstrates that the alpha-synuclein pathology leads to cortical atrophy through neuronal loss, particularly pronounced in cortical and limbic regions.

steps/2.description: Progressive loss of neurons due to alpha-synuclein pathology and associated proteinopathies, leading to brain atrophy particularly in cortical and limbic regions. The neurodegeneration underlies the progressive cognitive decline and other clinical features of DLB.

evidence.snippet: The clinical features of DLB and PDD include cognitive impairment, parkinsonism, visual hallucinations, and fluctuating attention.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that cognitive impairment with characteristic fluctuating attention is a core feature of dementia with Lewy bodies.

evidence.snippet: DLB shares risk loci with AD, in the APOE E4 allele, and with PD, in variation at GBA and SNCA.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that the APOE ε4 allele is a shared genetic risk locus between DLB and Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Intravitam PET and post-mortem studies revealed more pronounced cortical atrophy, elevated cortical and limbic Lewy pathologies (with APOE ε4).
evidence.explanation: This demonstrates that APOE ε4 is associated with more pronounced Lewy pathology in DLB.

genes/0.notes: The APOE ε4 allele increases risk for DLB and is associated with more pronounced cortical Lewy pathology and higher prevalence of concomitant Alzheimer pathology. APOE represents a shared genetic risk factor between DLB and Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: GBA variants increased the risk of DLB, especially N370S, E326K, and L444P which are strongly associated with DLB, but T369M was not. Patients harbouring GBA variants have an earlier age of onset, more severe cognitive impairment, and rapid symptom progression.
evidence.explanation: This meta-analysis confirms that specific GBA variants are strongly associated with DLB and correlate with earlier onset and more severe clinical presentation.

evidence.snippet: More recently, association and exome sequencing studies in larger groups have been conducted, and have shown that several variants in GBA and the APOE ε4 allele are important genetic risk factors for DLB.
evidence.explanation: This review confirms that GBA variants are important genetic risk factors for dementia with Lewy bodies.

evidence.snippet: DLB shares risk loci with AD, in the APOE E4 allele, and with PD, in variation at GBA and SNCA.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that GBA represents a shared genetic risk locus between DLB and Parkinson's disease.

genes/1.notes: Variants in the glucocerebrosidase (GBA) gene are important genetic risk factors for DLB. GBA mutation carriers have earlier age of onset, more severe cognitive impairment, and more rapid symptom progression. Specific variants including N370S, E326K, and L444P are strongly associated with DLB.

evidence.snippet: DLB shares risk loci with AD, in the APOE E4 allele, and with PD, in variation at GBA and SNCA.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that SNCA represents a shared genetic risk locus between DLB and Parkinson's disease.

genes/2.notes: The SNCA gene encoding alpha-synuclein shows genetic association with DLB, representing a shared genetic risk factor with Parkinson's disease. Variation at SNCA influences risk for developing Lewy body pathology.

evidence.snippet: Clinical management of both disorders includes cholinesterase inhibitors, other pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic strategies, but these have only a mild symptomatic effect.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that cholinesterase inhibitors are part of standard clinical management for DLB, though they provide only mild symptomatic benefit.

treatments/0.description: Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine, donepezil, and galantamine are used to manage cognitive symptoms in DLB. These medications address the cholinergic deficits present in the disease and can provide mild symptomatic benefit for cognitive and behavioral symptoms.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Cholinesterase inhibitors compensate for cholinergic neuronal loss caused by Lewy body pathology by enhancing synaptic acetylcholine availability, partially restoring cortical cholinergic tone in areas where neurons have been lost.

evidence.snippet: Currently, no disease-modifying therapies are available.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that no disease-modifying therapies are currently available for DLB, with treatment limited to symptomatic management.

treatments/1.description: No disease-modifying treatments currently available. Management focuses on symptomatic treatment of cognitive, motor, and psychiatric symptoms. Includes both pharmacological approaches (cautious use of antipsychotics due to sensitivity, dopaminergic therapy for parkinsonism) and non-pharmacological strategies including behavioral interventions and caregiver support.

evidence.snippet: The variant identified in the WS family changes an alanine residue conserved in all eukaryotic organisms and positioned within the tRNA-binding moiety of this nuclear genome-encoded mitochondrial translational elongation factor.
evidence.explanation: Locates the disease allele within the tRNA-binding region of mtEF4 and establishes the residue's conservation, the basis for treating it as the initiating lesion.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion is a homozygous GUF1 missense variant. In the reported family the allele is c.1825G>T, p.(Ala609Ser), which substitutes an alanine conserved across all eukaryotic organisms and positioned within the tRNA-binding moiety of the protein. Note that the functional consequence is reported as a modification of activity under suboptimal conditions rather than as a clean null, so this node is deliberately not labelled a loss of function.

evidence.snippet: GUF1 encodes a protein essential in conditions that counteract faithful protein synthesis: it is able to remobilize stuck ribosomes and transiently inhibit the elongation process to optimize protein synthesis.
evidence.explanation: States the molecular role of the gene product that this node models. Evidence source is OTHER because the sentence is background molecular biology synthesised from model-system work, not a clinical observation made in this study.

evidence.snippet: The observed defects in Guf1-deficient mitochondria are consistent with a function of Guf1 as a fidelity factor of mitochondrial protein synthesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the fidelity-factor role in the yeast ortholog, the conserved function whose disruption this node describes.

evidence.snippet: It binds to mitochondrial ribosomes in a GTP-dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: Supports the GTPase and ribosome-engagement molecular function annotated on this node.

evidence.snippet: Deletion of mtEF4 accelerated mitochondrial translation at the cost of producing unstable proteins.
evidence.explanation: The mammalian in vivo result, and the reason this node asserts a fidelity defect without asserting a direction of rate change: here loss of mtEF4 speeds translation up rather than slowing it.

steps/2.description: GUF1/mtEF4 is a quality-control factor of mitochondrial protein synthesis rather than a core elongation engine: it binds mitoribosomes in a GTP-dependent manner, remobilizes stalled ribosomes, and transiently inhibits elongation so that synthesis remains accurate.
