evidence.snippet: Mice expressing the collagen X mutation had shortened limbs and an expanded hypertrophic zone.
evidence.explanation: Hypertrophic zone expansion is a hallmark finding in the knock-in mouse model.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that COL10A1 mutations result in a uniform pattern of growth plate abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Supports growth plate dysfunction as a uniform consequence of COL10A1 mutations in human patients.

steps/4.description: Impaired vascular clearance of the hypertrophic zone leads to accumulation of undegraded hypertrophic chondrocytes and expansion of the hypertrophic zone, resulting in metaphyseal abnormalities and impaired longitudinal bone growth.

evidence.snippet: We show that nonsense/frame-shift mutations can elicit a gain-of-function effect, affecting chondrocyte differentiation in the growth plate.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that nonsense/frameshift alleles act by gain of function on chondrocyte differentiation rather than purely by reducing collagen X dosage.

evidence.snippet: Thus for both classes of mutations, functional haploinsufficiency is the most probable cause of the clinical phenotype in SMCD.
evidence.explanation: Supports the reduction in functional extracellular collagen X across mutation classes. Marked PARTIAL because the review's further conclusion that this reduction is the cause of the phenotype is superseded by the Col10a1-null comparison and the ER-stress-sufficiency experiment.

steps/5.description: All MCDS mutation classes lower the amount of functional collagen X reaching the hypertrophic-zone matrix: nonsense alleles may be degraded by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, while missense and frameshift alleles remove their product from the matrix by intracellular retention. This dosage reduction is a real consequence of the mutation but is not by itself sufficient to produce the disease. Col10a1 null animals, which have the dosage defect without a mutant chain, do not reproduce MCDS, whereas animals expressing a mutant chain do. The phenotype is therefore attributed to the gain-of-function ER stress response (see mechanistic_hypotheses: er_stress_gain_of_function), with the older haploinsufficiency reading retained as a deprecated hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a 13 base pair deletion in one type X collagen allele segregating with autosomal dominant Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia in a large Mormon kindred (lod score = 18.2 at theta = 0).
evidence.explanation: Original identification of COL10A1 as the causal gene.

evidence.snippet: Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (SMCD) is a dominantly inherited cartilage disorder caused by mutations in the gene for the hypertrophic cartilage extracellular matrix structural protein, collagen X (COL10A1).
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive review consolidating the causal gene-disease relationship and mutation spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Mutations, mostly in the region of the COL10A1 gene encoding the C-terminal non-collagenous domain, cause the dwarfism metaphyseal chondrodysplasia type Schmid (MCDS).
evidence.explanation: Background statement from a mouse model study confirming NC1 domain as the primary mutation hotspot.

evidence.snippet: The expression of type X collagen is restricted to hypertrophic chondrocytes in regions undergoing endochondral ossification, such as growth plates.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the tissue-restricted expression pattern of COL10A1.

evidence.snippet: Genotype-phenotype analysis of 124 cases previously reported and 4 new cases revealed that NC1 domain mutations were associated with an earlier onset of MCDS than non-NC1 mutations (median 12 vs. 72 months, P = 0.0014). Patients carrying a missense mutation in COL10A1 showed significantly lower height Z-scores (- 3.62 ± 1.95 vs. - 1.99 ± 1.28, P = 0.013) at first and more metaphyseal irregularities in the distal radius/ulna than those with truncating mutations (P = 0.019).
evidence.explanation: Large genotype-phenotype analysis demonstrating NC1 domain mutations associate with earlier onset and missense mutations with more severe short stature.

evidence.snippet: COL10A1 | HGNC:2185 | Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia | MONDO:0007983 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the COL10A1-Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia gene-disease relationship as definitive with autosomal dominant inheritance.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in COL10A1 cause MCDS. Most mutations cluster in the NC1 (non-collagenous) domain. Missense, nonsense, and frameshift mutations are all represented. Type X collagen expression is restricted to hypertrophic chondrocytes during endochondral ossification.

evidence.snippet: corrective osteotomy by guided growth surgery or valgus osteotomy may be considered in late childhood / adolescence in those with progressive or symptomatic varus deformity, significant coxa vara, triangular fragment in the interior femoral neck, or poor or deteriorating function
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommendations for surgical intervention.

evidence.snippet: Osteotomies to correct bow legs are sometimes combined with lengthening procedures. Recurrence of the deformities with growth is not uncommon; therefore, hemiepiphysiodesis or stapling might be indicated in some cases.
evidence.explanation: Describes orthopedic surgical experience including risk of deformity recurrence.

evidence.snippet: Six patients had lower limb deformities, which necessitated orthopedic surgeries in all of them.
evidence.explanation: Confirms orthopedic surgery needed in patients with significant deformity.

treatments/0.description: Corrective osteotomy (guided growth surgery or valgus osteotomy) may be considered in late childhood or adolescence for progressive or symptomatic varus deformity, significant coxa vara, or deteriorating function. Recurrence of deformities with growth is not uncommon.

evidence.snippet: Management of orthopedic complications by an orthopedist, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, and pain specialist as indicated; joint-friendly exercise, weight management; mobility device as needed
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management recommendations for supportive care.

treatments/1.description: Management includes physiotherapy, occupational therapy, joint-friendly exercise, weight management, and psychosocial support. Mobility devices may be needed. Obesity and physical activities causing excessive joint strain should be avoided.

evidence.snippet: Once the COL10A1 pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal testing for a pregnancy at increased risk for SMCD and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews genetic counseling section.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling is recommended given autosomal dominant inheritance with 50% recurrence risk. Prenatal testing and preimplantation genetic testing are available once the familial COL10A1 variant is identified.

evidence.snippet: treatment of the mice with carbamazepine (CBZ), a drug which stimulates intracellular proteolysis and alleviates ER stress, effectively reduced the disease severity in this model of MCDS caused by a premature stop codon in the Col10a1 gene. Specifically, the drug reduced ER stress in the growth plate, restored growth plate architecture toward the wild-type state, significantly increased bone growth and within 2 weeks of treatment corrected the MCDS-induced hip distortion.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical evidence of carbamazepine efficacy in MCDS mouse model.

treatments/3.description: Carbamazepine, which stimulates intracellular proteolysis and alleviates ER stress, reduced disease severity in a mouse model of MCDS. The drug reduced ER stress in the growth plate, restored growth plate architecture, increased bone growth, and corrected hip distortion within two weeks of treatment. This remains preclinical.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of mutant mice with a chemical inhibitor of PERK signaling prevents the differentiation defects and ameliorates chondrodysplasia. By preventing aberrant differentiation, titrated inhibition of the ISR emerges as a rationale therapeutic strategy for stress-induced skeletal disorders.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical evidence of PERK pathway inhibition as a therapeutic approach.

treatments/4.description: Chemical inhibition of the PERK signaling pathway prevented differentiation defects and ameliorated chondrodysplasia in a mouse model, suggesting that titrated ISR inhibition may be a therapeutic strategy for MCDS. This remains preclinical.

evidence.snippet: Unlike Col10a1 null mutants, transgenic mice (FCdel) bearing the mouse equivalent of a human MCDS p.P620fsX621 mutation, displayed typical characteristics of MCDS with disproportionate shortening of limbs and early onset coxa vara.
evidence.explanation: The decisive comparison: null (dosage-reduced) animals do not reproduce MCDS, whereas animals expressing a mutant chain do, arguing against haploinsufficiency as the operative mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Our data demonstrate that triggering ER stress per se in hypertrophic chondrocytes is sufficient to induce the essential features of the cartilage pathology associated with MCDS and confirm that ER stress is a central pathogenic factor in the disease mechanism.
evidence.explanation: ER stress alone, induced by an unrelated protein, is sufficient to produce the MCDS cartilage phenotype.

hypotheses/0.description: Mutant collagen X misfolds and is retained in the ER of hypertrophic chondrocytes, and the resulting ER stress and UPR (dominantly the PERK arm) reverts chondrocyte differentiation and expands the hypertrophic zone. This is a gain of function of the mutant chain, not a loss of collagen X dosage.

evidence.snippet: Thus for both classes of mutations, functional haploinsufficiency is the most probable cause of the clinical phenotype in SMCD.
evidence.explanation: The 2005 review statement of the haploinsufficiency model, recorded here as the source of the superseded hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: We show that nonsense/frame-shift mutations can elicit a gain-of-function effect, affecting chondrocyte differentiation in the growth plate.
evidence.explanation: Directly against the haploinsufficiency model: the mutation classes it claimed act purely by dosage reduction are shown to act by gain of function.

hypotheses/1.description: An earlier model in which the shared proximate cause across MCDS mutation classes is a reduction in functional extracellular collagen X: nonsense alleles are degraded by nonsense-mediated decay, and missense/frameshift alleles remove their product from the matrix by intracellular retention.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in structural subunits and assembly factors of complex I of the oxidative phosphorylation system constitute the most common cause of mitochondrial respiratory chain defects.
evidence.explanation: The disease class this variant places the patient in, and why a complex I subunit was a credible candidate.

steps/1.description: A homozygous c.113-10C>G change in an NDUFB7 intron, ten bases upstream of the acceptor site. This is the class of variant that routine filtering discards: it is not coding, not canonical splice-site, and would be scored by most in silico splice predictors rather than observed. It was found by whole genome sequencing and taken seriously because the RNA was sequenced too.

evidence.snippet: splicing pattern alterations in NDUFB7 messenger RNA were confirmed by RNA Sequencing
evidence.explanation: The transcript-level measurement this node records.

steps/2.description: Splicing pattern alterations confirmed by RNA sequencing of patient material. The measurement matters more than usual here: for a non-canonical intronic variant, the transcript is the only place the effect is visible, and predicting it would not have been the same claim.

evidence.snippet: The detected variant resulted in a significant reduction of the NDUFB7 protein and reduced complex I activity.
evidence.explanation: The protein-level measurement, reported together with the enzymatic one it produces.

evidence.snippet: Bacterial and human complex I share 14 core subunits that are essential for enzymatic function; however, the role and necessity of the remaining 31 human accessory subunits is unclear.
evidence.explanation: Places NDUFB7 in the accessory rather than the core class, which is what determines whether its loss is expected to abolish catalysis directly or to act through assembly.

steps/3.description: The accessory subunit falls in abundance. NDUFB7 is one of the thirty-one accessory subunits of the forty-five-subunit human enzyme, and is not among the fourteen core subunits shared with bacterial complex I that carry catalysis.

evidence.snippet: Quantitative proteomic analysis of cell lines revealed that loss of each subunit affects the stability of other subunits residing in the same structural module.
evidence.explanation: The module-destabilisation principle that connects a reduced accessory subunit to a failed enzyme. Measured across the accessory subunit knockout panel, not specifically on NDUFB7.

evidence.snippet: We show that 25 subunits are strictly required for assembly of a functional complex and 1 subunit is essential for cell viability.
evidence.explanation: How often the principle holds, which sets the prior for NDUFB7 being one of the required ones. It also leaves six accessory subunits that are not, so this is a strong prior and not a demonstration.

steps/4.description:
The step from a missing subunit to a broken enzyme. A systematic knockout screen of every accessory subunit found that losing any one of them destabilises the other subunits sitting in the same structural module, and that twenty-five of the thirty-one are strictly required for a functional complex to assemble at all.
That is the mechanism this node asserts, and it is asserted as a general property of accessory subunits rather than as a measurement on NDUFB7. The cached record of the screen reports the rule across subunits without naming NDUFB7's module or its individual result, and no complexome profile has been published for a MC1DN39 patient. The node is marked PROVISIONAL for that reason.

evidence.snippet: Complementation studies with expression of wild-type NDUFB7 in patient fibroblasts normalized complex I function.
evidence.explanation: The rescue experiment. This is the strongest single piece of evidence in the entry because it tests the gene against the phenotype within one patient's own cells.

steps/5.description: Complex I activity is reduced with the other respiratory chain complexes intact, which is what makes the deficiency isolated. This node is where the causal argument closes: expressing wild-type NDUFB7 in the patient's own fibroblasts normalised complex I function, so the enzyme defect is attributable to NDUFB7 and not to an unrelated variant carried by the same patient.

evidence.snippet: We describe a patient presenting intrauterine growth restriction and anemia, which displayed postpartum hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis, encephalopathy, and a severe complex I defect with fatal outcome.
evidence.explanation: The clinical presentation this node produces, in the one patient in whom it has been observed.

evidence.snippet: Complex I deficiency caused by a nuclear gene defect is usually a non-dysmorphic syndrome, characterized by severe multi-system organ involvement and a poor prognosis.
evidence.explanation: The multi-system pattern across the nuclear complex I deficiency group, which is the comparison class for a single patient's presentation.

steps/6.description:
Reduced electron transfer through complex I lowers oxidative phosphorylation output, and the tissues that decompensate first are the ones with the highest ATP demand: heart and brain. The clinical picture in the index patient follows that pattern, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy, and the anaerobic compensation shows as lactic acidosis.
The tissue-selectivity reasoning is standard mitochondrial-medicine inference rather than a measurement in this patient, so the node is marked PROVISIONAL. No cardiac or brain tissue enzymology was reported.

evidence.snippet: We describe a patient presenting intrauterine growth restriction and anemia, which displayed postpartum hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis, encephalopathy, and a severe complex I defect with fatal outcome.
evidence.explanation: The clinical description in which this phenotype is reported.

steps/7.description: Severe congenital lactic acidosis, the biochemical hallmark of the bioenergetic block. Present from the neonatal period in the index patient.

evidence.snippet: We describe a patient presenting intrauterine growth restriction and anemia, which displayed postpartum hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis, encephalopathy, and a severe complex I defect with fatal outcome.
evidence.explanation: The cardiac phenotype in the index patient.

steps/8.description: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy appearing after birth. Cardiac involvement is not universal in nuclear complex I deficiency, and the 130-case series found that defects in some genes seem to associate with cardiomyopathy while others do not, so its prominence here is a candidate gene-specific feature rather than a generic one. With one patient it cannot be more than a candidate.

evidence.snippet: Virtually all children ultimately develop Leigh syndrome or leukoencephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: The neurological trajectory of the group. Cited for the class rather than this subtype, because the index patient died before a trajectory could be observed.

steps/9.description: Neonatal encephalopathy. Brain involvement is near-universal across nuclear complex I deficiency, where the 130-case series found that virtually all children ultimately develop Leigh syndrome or leukoencephalopathy; no neuroimaging pattern has been reported for this subtype.

evidence.snippet: Whole genome sequencing revealed an intronic biallelic mutation in the NDUFB7 gene (c.113-10C>G) and splicing pattern alterations in NDUFB7 messenger RNA were confirmed by RNA Sequencing.
evidence.explanation: Evidence for this specific edge: the same sentence reports the variant and the measured splicing consequence, which is what makes the intronic change actionable rather than a candidate.

evidence.snippet: Complementation studies with expression of wild-type NDUFB7 in patient fibroblasts normalized complex I function.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease evidence is a rescue rather than a segregation argument, which is what a single consanguineous family can offer and is arguably stronger for causality than a small pedigree would be.

genes/0.notes: The causal gene, encoding an accessory subunit of complex I. Not one of the fourteen core subunits, which matters mechanistically: the route from a reduced accessory subunit to a failed enzyme runs through assembly and module stability rather than through direct loss of catalytic capacity.

evidence.snippet: Treatment for mitochondrial diseases remains largely symptomatic and does not significantly alter the course of the disease.
evidence.explanation: The state of mitochondrial disease therapy, from a review of the field. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a narrative review rather than a study, and it is cited for the class this disease belongs to rather than for this disease.

treatments/0.description:
There is no disease-modifying therapy for MC1DN39, and none for nuclear complex I deficiency generally. Management is symptomatic: treating the lactic acidosis, the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and the encephalopathy as they present.
This block records the state of the field rather than anything reported for a MC1DN39 patient. No treatment or treatment response was described for the index case, and with one patient no disease-specific management claim is possible.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Supportive care addresses the organ consequences of the bioenergetic failure. It does not act on the assembly defect, and nothing reported does.

evidence.snippet: Therapeutic strategies for mitochondrial diseases include the use of agents enhancing electron transfer chain function (coenzyme Q10, idebenone, riboflavin, dichloroacetate, and thiamine), agents acting as energy buffer (creatine), antioxidants (vitamin C, vitamin E, lipoic acid, cysteine donors, and EPI-743), amino acids restoring nitric oxide production (arginine and citrulline), cardiolipin protector (elamipretide), agents enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis (bezafibrate, epicatechin, and RTA 408), nucleotide bypass therapy, liver transplantation, and gene therapy.
evidence.explanation: The agents in question and the category they are placed in. Cited for what is used in the field, not for efficacy in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: Based on limited number of clinical trials, several agents aiming at enhancing mitochondrial function or treating the consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction have been used.
evidence.explanation: The strength of the evidence base behind these agents, in the reviewers' own words. Quoted here rather than paraphrased because the hedge is the point.

treatments/1.description:
The vitamin and cofactor combination often given in mitochondrial disease, typically including riboflavin, coenzyme Q10, thiamine and carnitine. It is offered because the alternative is nothing, not because it has been shown to work: the reviewed evidence base is a small number of clinical trials across a heterogeneous group of disorders, and no trial has enrolled a patient with this genotype.
Riboflavin has a mechanistic rationale specific to complex I, since flavin mononucleotide is the enzyme's own NADH-oxidising prosthetic group, but that rationale is not a result. Nothing here should be read as evidence of benefit in MC1DN39.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: The stated aim is to enhance residual electron transfer chain function rather than to restore complex I assembly. Whether that is achievable when the enzyme cannot be assembled is exactly the untested question.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-five percent of the patients died before the age of six months, more than half before the age of two and 75 % before the age of ten years.
evidence.explanation: The survival distribution across the group, which is wide.

evidence.snippet: No clinical, biochemical, or genetic parameters indicating longer survival were found.
evidence.explanation: That nothing measured predicts position within that range, which is what makes a single case uninformative about prognosis.

evidence.snippet: Such mutations can present a wide range of clinical manifestations, varying from mild deficiencies to severe, lethal disorders.
evidence.explanation: The reporting authors say the same thing about complex I mutations generally, in the paper describing the fatal case.

open_questions/0.rationale:
This is the gap most likely to be answered wrongly by inference, because a single fatal case reads as a prognosis unless something stops it.
The group-level data say stop. Across 130 patients with nuclear gene defects causing complex I deficiency, a quarter died before six months and three quarters before ten years, but some recovered skills and some were alive in their thirties, and the authors reported that no clinical, biochemical or genetic parameter predicted longer survival. A range that wide, with no predictor, means one observation carries almost no information about the next patient.
There is also a specific reason to expect variability for this gene in particular. The reported allele is an intronic splicing variant, which produces a quantitative rather than an absolute reduction in protein; a different NDUFB7 allele producing a different residual level could plausibly give a different course. That is speculation, but it is speculation the evidence base cannot currently rule out, which is precisely why the entry does not state a prognosis.
A note on how the fatal outcome is recorded. It is not curated as a phenotype: HP:0003811 Neonatal death sits under HPO's mortality branch rather than under Phenotypic abnormality, so it is outside the PhenotypeTerm dynamic enum and cannot be bound in a phenotypes entry. The outcome therefore lives in this discussion and in the entry description, which is the right place for it given that it is one observation rather than a disease feature, but the constraint is the schema's rather than a curation decision.

evidence.snippet: Here we use gene editing to generate human knockout cell lines for each accessory subunit.
evidence.explanation: The screen covers every accessory subunit, so an NDUFB7-specific answer exists in principle; what the cached record does not carry is that answer.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The entry's causal chain has one link that is not measured for this gene, and it is worth naming rather than leaving a reader to notice.
The knockout screen established a rule: losing an accessory subunit destabilises the other subunits in its own structural module, and twenty-five of thirty-one accessory subunits are strictly required for a functional complex. The record cached for this entry states the rule and the count without naming NDUFB7's module or reporting its individual result, so the entry applies a strong prior rather than a finding. Six accessory subunits are not strictly required, and nothing here excludes NDUFB7 being one of them, with the enzyme defect in this patient arising some other way.
Two things would close it and neither is expensive. The screen's own supplementary data almost certainly contain the NDUFB7 knockout line's result, which would settle the general question immediately. A complexome profile or blue native analysis of the patient's fibroblasts, which already exist and already showed the enzyme defect, would settle the specific one and say whether assembly stalls at an identifiable intermediate.

evidence.snippet: Whole genome sequencing revealed an intronic biallelic mutation in the NDUFB7 gene (c.113-10C>G) and splicing pattern alterations in NDUFB7 messenger RNA were confirmed by RNA Sequencing.
evidence.explanation: The two technologies that were needed to find and confirm this variant, neither of which is standard first-line testing.

open_questions/2.rationale:
Worth recording because it bears on why this disorder has one patient, and the answer is not necessarily that it is vanishingly rare.
A c.113-10C>G change is outside the coding sequence and outside the canonical splice dinucleotides. Exome capture may not cover it well, standard variant filtering usually discards it, and in silico splice prediction is the only thing that would flag it. This case was solved because the group ran whole genome sequencing and then sequenced the RNA to check what the variant actually did. A laboratory doing exome-only analysis with coding filters would have found nothing in this patient.
So the reported frequency of MC1DN39 is a statement about how the group has been ascertained as much as about how often the disease occurs. Re-analysis of unsolved isolated complex I deficiency cohorts with genome sequencing plus RNA sequencing is the obvious test, and it is the same test that would answer the prognosis gap above by supplying more patients.

evidence.snippet: Asp57 is invariant in all defined GTP-binding proteins. Rac2(D57N) binds GDP but not GTP and inhibits oxidase activation and O(2)(-) production in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the nucleotide-binding defect and its inhibitory - not merely absent - effect on oxidase activation.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies demonstrated that the D57N mutant behaves in a dominant-negative fashion at the cellular level.
evidence.explanation: Direct support for the DOMINANT_NEGATIVE functional impact category rather than a loss-of-function assignment.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion. Asp57 is invariant across GTP-binding proteins and participates directly in nucleotide binding. The mutant protein binds GDP but not GTP, so it is locked in the inactive conformation, and it acts dominant-negatively rather than as a simple null: it sequesters guanine nucleotide exchange factors and effectors away from the wild-type protein. That is why one allele is enough.

evidence.snippet: Addition of recombinant Rac to extracts of the patient neutrophils reconstituted O(2)(-) production in an in vitro assay system.
evidence.explanation: A reconstitution result: the oxidase machinery itself is intact and only its RAC2 activator is missing, which is the mechanistic distinction from chronic granulomatous disease.

evidence.snippet: Most mutants produced elevated superoxide; mutations unable to support superoxide formation were associated with bacterial infections.
evidence.explanation: Across the whole RAC2 allele spectrum, inability to support superoxide formation is what tracks with bacterial infection. That separates the dominant-negative arm curated here from the majority of RAC2 alleles, which raise superoxide instead - so the oxidase failure is specific to this arm rather than generic to the gene.

steps/2.description: The first of the two effector arms. RAC2 is required for activation of the NOX2 NADPH oxidase, and the D57N protein inhibits oxidase activation in vitro. The defect is at the level of the ACTIVATOR, not the catalytic complex, which is what distinguishes this from chronic granulomatous disease even though the downstream consequence - failed respiratory burst - is shared. The decisive reconstitution experiment is that adding recombinant Rac to patient neutrophil extracts restores superoxide production.

evidence.snippet: Neutrophils from this patient exhibited decreased chemotaxis, polarization, azurophilic granule secretion, and superoxide anion (O(2)(-)) production but had normal expression and up-regulation of CD11b.
evidence.explanation: Documents both effector arms failing in the same patient, and the normal CD11b that excludes leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I.

evidence.snippet: rac2-/- neutrophils displayed significant defects in chemotaxis, in shear-dependent L-selectin-mediated capture on the endothelial substrate Glycam-1, and in both F-actin generation and p38 and, unexpectedly, p42/p44 MAP kinase activation induced by chemoattractants.
evidence.explanation: Resolves the migration arm into its component steps - capture, actin assembly and MAP kinase signalling - in the knockout mouse.

steps/3.description: The second effector arm, and the one chronic granulomatous disease does not have. Patient neutrophils show decreased chemotaxis, polarization and azurophilic granule secretion. In the Rac2-null mouse the same arm fails through defective F-actin generation, impaired p38 and p42/p44 MAP kinase activation, and loss of shear-dependent L-selectin-mediated capture, so the defect spans capture, polarization and migration rather than any single step. This is curated as a separate node from the oxidase arm rather than bundled into one "neutrophil dysfunction" node, because the two are independent effector routes from the same GTPase.

evidence.snippet: These defects were reflected in vivo by baseline neutrophilia, reduced inflammatory peritoneal exudate formation, and increased mortality when challenged with Aspergillus fumigatus.
evidence.explanation: The mouse correlate of "leukocytosis without pus": neutrophilia in blood with failure to form a tissue exudate, plus a host-defence consequence.

steps/4.description: The two arms converge here, and the convergence explains the syndrome's most distinctive feature: peripheral neutrophilia coexisting with an absence of neutrophils where they are needed. Neutrophils are produced and released normally but do not accumulate at infected sites, so infections proceed without pus formation and wounds heal poorly. The Rac2-null mouse reproduces exactly this pairing - baseline neutrophilia in the blood alongside reduced inflammatory peritoneal exudate.

evidence.snippet: A 5-week-old male infant presented with severe bacterial infections and poor wound healing, suggesting a neutrophil defect.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the age and mode of presentation.

evidence.snippet: Despite features suggesting a neutrophil disorder, results of screening tests of phagocyte function were normal.
evidence.explanation: The diagnostic trap: routine phagocyte screening does not detect this disease, which is why it is missed despite a suggestive clinical picture.

evidence.snippet: A novel, multifaceted leukocyte disorder-distinguished by defects in shape change, chemotaxis, ingestion, degranulation, superoxide anion production, and bactericidal activity-was established secondary to a defect in Rac2.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates six distinct human neutrophil functions that fail, which is the clinical expression of one GTPase serving two effector arms - shape change, chemotaxis and ingestion on the actin side; degranulation, superoxide and bactericidal activity on the killing side.

evidence.snippet: The case of an infant with multiple, rapidly progressive, soft-tissue infections is presented.
evidence.explanation: The clinical setting in which the failure of tissue neutrophil function shows itself.

steps/5.description: The clinical presentation, in the index case at five weeks of age. Routine screening tests are normal, so the diagnosis is easily missed: the neutrophil count is high rather than low, CD11b is normal, and the defect is functional rather than numerical.

evidence.snippet: A 5-week-old male infant presented with severe bacterial infections and poor wound healing, suggesting a neutrophil defect.
evidence.explanation: The presenting infection phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Group 2 consisted of 5 patients who presented within the first month of life with omphalitis, abscesses, and periumbilical erythema with decreased T cells and B cells and normal or elevated neutrophil counts due to DN D57N mutation.
evidence.explanation: Human evidence for the count, specific to the dominant-negative D57N arm this entry covers. It says "normal or elevated", which is why the node claims that rather than uniform neutrophilia, and why the more committed term HP:0410258 "Neutrophilia in absence of infection" is not used - these patients were described mid-infection.

evidence.snippet: These defects were reflected in vivo by baseline neutrophilia, reduced inflammatory peritoneal exudate formation, and increased mortality when challenged with Aspergillus fumigatus.
evidence.explanation: The knockout mouse shows frank BASELINE neutrophilia - a stronger and differently qualified claim than the human "normal or elevated", since it is measured without infection. Recorded as PARTIAL so the model's extra commitment is not read back onto the human phenotype.

steps/7.description: Neutrophil counts are not low. That is the diagnostically counterintuitive part and a direct consequence of the mechanism: production and release are intact while tissue recruitment fails, so an infected patient does not present with the neutropenia the clinical picture might suggest. The human cohort describes counts as "normal or elevated" rather than uniformly raised, and this node is worded to that claim rather than to the stronger one the disease name (immunodeficiency 73A with leukocytosis) implies.

evidence.snippet: Neutrophils from this patient exhibited decreased chemotaxis, polarization, azurophilic granule secretion, and superoxide anion (O(2)(-)) production but had normal expression and up-regulation of CD11b.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents impaired chemotaxis in patient neutrophils.

evidence.snippet: Rac2(D57N) binds GDP but not GTP and inhibits oxidase activation and O(2)(-) production in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Documents the oxidative burst defect and its molecular cause.

edges/1.description: RAC2 is the GTPase component required to activate the NADPH oxidase; the GDP-locked mutant cannot deliver that activation and actively inhibits it.

edges/2.description: The same GTPase drives chemoattractant-induced actin polymerization and polarization, so one allele disables a second, independent effector arm.

edges/3.description: The assay measurement of this node, and the finding that makes this disease look like CGD on a DHR test despite a different lesion.

edges/4.description: Loss of the respiratory burst removes oxidative microbial killing.

edges/5.description: The assay measurement of this node.

edges/6.description: Loss of directed migration prevents neutrophils reaching the site of infection.

edges/7.description: The count is normal or high precisely because release is intact and function is not — the finding that distinguishes this disease from congenital neutropenia and the one most likely to mislead.

edges/8.description: Failure of tissue neutrophil function permits uncontrolled bacterial infection.

edges/9.description: The clinical expression of neutrophils that reach neither the site nor the kill.

evidence.snippet: Molecular methods were used to clone the expressed Rac2 cDNA from this patient, and a single base pair change (G-->A at nucleotide 169) in the coding sequence was identified. This results in an asparagine for aspartic acid mutation at amino acid 57 (D57N), a residue that is involved in nucleotide binding and is conserved in all mammalian Rho GTPases.
evidence.explanation: Gives the nucleotide-level change and the conservation of the affected residue, quoted verbatim because secondary summaries of this variant's cDNA nomenclature disagree with the source.

genes/0.notes: Quote the nucleotide change from the primary source. Secondary summaries render this variant inconsistently, and at least one renders it as a C to A change, which contradicts the source's own "G to A at nucleotide 169".

evidence.snippet: Most patients with constitutively active and DN disease underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) within the first months (constitutively active) to first year (DN D57N) of life
evidence.explanation: Documents HSCT as the standard course for dominant-negative disease and the age at which it is undertaken.

treatments/0.description: The definitive therapy. RAC2 is expressed only in haematopoietic cells, so replacing the haematopoietic compartment replaces the entire diseased tissue - there is no other organ carrying the lesion. In the RAC2 cohort most patients with dominant-negative disease were transplanted within the first year of life.

evidence.snippet: Rac2, which constitutes >96% of the Rac in neutrophils, is a member of the Rho family of GTPases that regulates the actin cytoskeleton and O(2)(-) production.
evidence.explanation: RAC2 carries essentially all Rac function in the neutrophil, so replacing the haematopoietic compartment replaces the whole diseased tissue rather than correcting part of it.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Acts at the initiating node by replacing the cells that express the mutant allele, rather than on any downstream effector arm. This is why it is curative where symptomatic measures are not.

evidence.snippet: The case of an infant with multiple, rapidly progressive, soft-tissue infections is presented.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the infection burden that antimicrobial management addresses.

treatments/1.description: Supportive rather than corrective. Because the neutrophils cannot reach or kill, bacterial infection is aggressive and rapidly progressive, so antimicrobial management is the mainstay until transplantation.

evidence.snippet: Disease correlated to RAC2 activity: constitutively active RAS-like mutations caused neonatal SCID, dominant-negative mutations caused LAD-like disease, whereas dominant-activating mutations caused CID.
evidence.explanation: The genotype-to-phenotype mapping that defines the scope boundary of this entry, from a 54-patient cohort in which every variant was functionally assayed.

evidence.snippet: Patients were grouped by presentation: neonatal SCID (n = 5), infantile LAD-like disease (n = 5), or CID (n = 44).
evidence.explanation: Gives the relative sizes of the three arms, showing the dominant-negative LAD-like arm curated here is the smallest.

open_questions/0.rationale: This entry deliberately covers only the dominant-negative arm. The definitive cohort separates the spectrum by RAC2 activity: constitutively active RAS-like alleles cause neonatal SCID, dominant-negative alleles cause the LAD-like disease curated here, and dominant-activating alleles cause a later-onset combined immunodeficiency, which accounted for 44 of 54 patients. Those are different graphs and should not be blended into this one. MONDO already gives IMD73B and IMD73C separate terms under a shared RAC2 combined-immunodeficiency parent, so the natural shape is one further Disease entry for the CID entity with 73B and 73C as subtypes; the constitutively active neonatal SCID arm appears to have no distinct MONDO term. Curating those is out of scope here and is left explicit rather than implied by omission.

evidence.snippet: Disease correlated to RAC2 activity: constitutively active RAS-like mutations caused neonatal SCID, dominant-negative mutations caused LAD-like disease, whereas dominant-activating mutations caused CID.
evidence.explanation: Assigns the SCID presentation to a different allele class from the one this MONDO term denotes, which is the basis for questioning the parent.

open_questions/1.rationale: MONDO gives this term two parents: functional neutrophil defect, which fits, and T-B- severe combined immunodeficiency, which does not obviously fit the dominant-negative arm. The cohort data place the dominant-negative alleles in the phagocyte/LAD-like group with normal-to-elevated neutrophil counts, while the T-B- SCID picture belongs to the constitutively active alleles at the same gene. This looks like gene-level classification applied to an allele-level term. Recorded here rather than acted on, because it is an upstream ontology question; the whole IMD73 series shares that parent, so it is likely one fix rather than three.

evidence.snippet: Phosphoglucomutase 1 enzyme activity was markedly diminished in all patients.
evidence.explanation: The landmark cohort establishes that PGM1 variants cause a measurable enzymatic loss of function in affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: Phosphoglucomutase type 1 (PGM1) activity in muscle and fibroblasts was severely deficient and PGM1 in muscle was undetectable by Western blot.
evidence.explanation: Confirms loss of PGM1 protein and activity in patient muscle and fibroblasts, supporting a loss-of-function mechanism.

steps/1.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in PGM1 (1p31.3) abolish or severely reduce phosphoglucomutase-1 activity. PGM1 supplies the large majority of phosphoglucomutase activity in most tissues, and residual activity in patient fibroblasts or leukocytes is severely reduced (the 2021 consensus guideline, PMID:32681750, reports a range from undetectable to 20% of controls). Most reported alleles are missense and act by loss of function, often through catalytic impairment or local structural destabilization of the enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Phosphoglucomutase 1 (PGM1) is a key enzyme for the regulation of energy metabolism from glycogen and glycolysis, as it catalyzes the interconversion of glucose 1-phosphate and glucose 6-phosphate.
evidence.explanation: Defines the enzymatic reaction that is lost and places it at the glycogen / glycolysis junction.

evidence.snippet: Analyses of sugar metabolites in fibroblasts from patients revealed increased concentrations of galactose-1-phosphate and glucose-1 phosphate, as compared with fibroblasts from controls.
evidence.explanation: Direct metabolite measurement in patient fibroblasts showing accumulation upstream of the enzymatic block.

steps/2.description: Phosphoglucomutase-1 reversibly interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, the metabolic node that connects glycogen (via glucose-1-phosphate) to glycolysis and to the hexose-phosphate pool used for nucleotide-sugar synthesis. When this step is blocked, flux is disrupted in both directions: glucose-6-phosphate generated from a dietary glucose load cannot be routed into glycogen, and glucose-1-phosphate released from glycogen cannot enter glycolysis or gluconeogenic output.

evidence.snippet: In vitro studies before treatment showed N-glycan hyposialylation, altered O-linked glycans, abnormal lipid-linked oligosaccharide profile, and abnormal nucleotide sugars in patient fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the ER lipid-linked oligosaccharide abnormality and the underlying nucleotide-sugar disturbance in PGM1-CDG fibroblasts, the disorder-specific substitution for the module's type I trigger.

evidence.snippet: D-gal increased both UDP-Glc and UDP-Gal levels and improved lipid-linked oligosaccharide fractions in concert with improved glycosylation in PGM1-CDG.
evidence.explanation: Rescue of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide profile by restoring nucleotide sugars confirms that donor depletion, not a transferase defect, drives the ER arm.

steps/3.description: This is the type I (endoplasmic-reticulum) arm of the mixed glycosylation defect. Reduced glucose-1-phosphate limits UDP-glucose, the donor used for glucosylation of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor and for calnexin/calreticulin quality control. Patient fibroblasts show an abnormal lipid-linked oligosaccharide profile, and truncated or incompletely transferred precursors leave N-glycosylation sequons unoccupied - detected in serum as whole missing transferrin glycans. Unlike the canonical type I CDG, the deficient element is not a glycosyltransferase of the assembly line but the nucleotide-sugar donor supply upstream of it.

evidence.snippet: The ratio of UDP-galactose to UDP-glucose was decreased, suggesting that UDP-galactose is limiting for N-glycan biosynthesis
evidence.explanation: Establishes UDP-galactose as the limiting nucleotide sugar, the mechanistic basis of the galactose-deficient truncated glycans.

evidence.snippet: replenishes the depleted levels of galactose-1-P, as well as the levels of UDP-glucose and UDP-galactose, the nucleotide sugars that are required for ER- and GA-linked glycosylation, respectively
evidence.explanation: Tracer metabolomics assigns UDP-glucose to the ER arm and UDP-galactose to the Golgi arm, the two-arm split modeled by this node and its ER sibling.

steps/4.description: This is the type II (Golgi) arm. PGM1 deficiency stalls the Leloir pathway and lowers the UDP-galactose available to Golgi galactosyltransferases, so N-glycans that are transferred to protein cannot be completed: they lack terminal galactose and, consequently, the sialic acid that caps it. The UDP-galactose to UDP-glucose ratio is reduced in patient cells, and the resulting glycans are truncated rather than absent. This is the arm that oral D-galactose therapy targets directly.

evidence.snippet: Mass spectrometry of transferrin showed a loss of complete N-glycans and the presence of truncated glycans lacking galactose.
evidence.explanation: The defining mixed pattern: missing whole glycans (type I) together with galactose-deficient truncated glycans (type II).

evidence.snippet: PGM1 deficiency is increasingly recognized as a congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG), where reduced N-linked glycosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi is observed, resulting in both missing and truncated glycans (mixed type I and type II glycosylation defects)
evidence.explanation: Explicitly names the mixed type I plus type II classification and localizes the two arms to ER and Golgi. Tagged OTHER because this is the review framing in the paper's introduction rather than its own experimental result.

steps/5.description: The two arms converge on the diagnostic hallmark of PGM1-CDG: a mixed glycosylation defect in which serum transferrin simultaneously shows loss of complete N-glycans (type I, reduced site occupancy) and truncated glycans lacking galactose and terminal sialic acid (type II, incomplete processing). Very few CDG produce both patterns in one patient, and this combined signature on intact-transferrin mass spectrometry is the single most useful biochemical clue to the diagnosis. Because glycosylation modifies a large fraction of secreted and membrane proteins, the lesion degrades many unrelated client glycoproteins at once.

evidence.snippet: a glycoproteomic analysis unveiled broad glycosylation changes with significant alterations in sarcolemmal proteins including different subunits of laminin-211, which was confirmed by immunoblot analyses
evidence.explanation: Identifies sarcolemmal and matrix glycoprotein hypoglycosylation, laminin-211 in particular, as a specific molecular lesion in the PGM1-deficient myocardium.

steps/6.description: Arm (b) of the galactose-resistant cardiomyopathy hypothesis. Cardiac glycoproteomics in the Pgm2 conditional knockout shows broad changes in N-glycosylation concentrated on sarcolemmal and extracellular-matrix proteins, most prominently the laminin-211 subunits that couple the cardiomyocyte membrane to its basement membrane. Loss of this linkage is a recognized route to dilated cardiomyopathy independent of energy supply.

evidence.snippet: We show that severe loss of PGM1 activity causes blocked muscle glycogenolysis that mimics McArdle disease, but may also limit glycogen synthesis, which broadens the phenotypic spectrum of this disorder.
evidence.explanation: Direct in vivo exercise physiology in a patient demonstrating a blocked muscle glycogenolysis. Note the authors hedge the synthesis arm ("may also limit glycogen synthesis"), so the biosynthetic half of this node is the weaker of the two claims.

evidence.snippet: During fasting, liver glycogen cannot be converted into glucose via glucose-6-phosphate, and hypoglycemia may occur.
evidence.explanation: States the hepatic arm of the glycogen block and its link to fasting hypoglycemia.

steps/7.description: Loss of the PGM1 step blocks both arms of glycogen handling. In liver, stored glycogen cannot be converted to glucose during fasting; in skeletal muscle, glycogen cannot be rapidly mobilized for anaerobic glycolysis during exertion. The muscle physiology closely mimics McArdle disease, including a flat lactate response to ischemic forearm exercise and a second-wind phenomenon.

evidence.snippet: Forearm exercise elicited no increase in lactate, but an exaggerated increase in ammonia, and provoked a forearm contracture.
evidence.explanation: Classic physiological signature of a block in muscle glycogenolysis and glycolysis in a PGM1-deficient patient.

evidence.snippet: Subsequent analyses revealed a lower basal respiration and mitochondrial ATP production capacity in the knockout myoblasts and myotubes, which were not restored by D-galactose.
evidence.explanation: Establishes a galactose-resistant mitochondrial energetic deficit in PGM1-null muscle cells, distinct from the galactose-responsive glycosylation arm.

steps/8.description: Skeletal muscle cannot mobilize glycogen for rapid anaerobic ATP production, so exercise depends abnormally on fat oxidation and carbohydrate oxidation is blocked; forearm exercise produces no lactate rise but an exaggerated ammonia rise, and patients show the McArdle-like second wind. Beyond the glycogenolytic block, PGM1-null myoblasts and myotubes have reduced basal respiration and reduced mitochondrial ATP-production capacity that D-galactose does not correct, which is the leading explanation for why myopathy and rhabdomyolysis respond less completely to therapy than the glycosylation abnormalities do.

evidence.snippet: Proteomic analyses revealed depletion of Z-disk components, including LDB3.
evidence.explanation: Directly reports the Z-disk protein depletion this node represents, in patient-derived cardiomyocytes.

evidence.snippet: AlphaFold3 structural modeling predicted a direct interaction between PGM1 and LDB3, implicating PGM1 in Z-disk integrity, which was confirmed in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Supports a direct PGM1-LDB3 interaction as the structural basis for the node, with in-vitro confirmation of a computational prediction.

steps/9.description: Arm (c) of the galactose-resistant cardiomyopathy hypothesis, and the only arm evidenced in human patient-derived cardiomyocytes rather than in mouse or in skeletal-muscle surrogate cells. Untargeted proteomics of iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes from PGM1-deficient patients shows depletion of Z-disk components, LDB3 (ZASP/Cypher) among them, and AlphaFold3 modelling predicts a direct PGM1-LDB3 interaction that was then confirmed in vitro. This places a structural, sarcomeric role for PGM1 alongside its enzymatic one: the protein is not only a metabolic enzyme whose loss starves the myocyte, it is a binding partner whose loss destabilizes the Z-disk. Because the claim is about a protein-protein interaction rather than a nucleotide-sugar pool, no amount of oral galactose addresses it - which is the point of curating it as a separate arm.

evidence.snippet: Histological studies demonstrated excess glycogen accumulation and fibrosis, while ultrastructural analysis revealed Z-disk disarray and swollen/fragmented mitochondria, which was similar to the ultrastructural pathology in the cardiac explant of an individual with PGM1-CDG.
evidence.explanation: The cardiomyocyte-specific knockout mouse reproduces the human cardiac ultrastructural pathology, including the mitochondrial injury that defines this node, and matches a human cardiac explant.

evidence.snippet: In addition, we found decreased mitochondrial function in the heart of KO mice.
evidence.explanation: Direct functional demonstration of the cardiac mitochondrial deficit.

steps/10.description: Arm (a) of the galactose-resistant cardiomyopathy hypothesis. In the cardiomyocyte-specific Pgm2 (mouse PGM1 ortholog) knockout heart, glycogen accumulates in excess while mitochondria are swollen and fragmented and mitochondrial function falls, indicating that the failing myocardium has an energy-supply problem and not only a glycosylation problem. The parallel finding in PGM1-null skeletal muscle cells, where D-galactose does not restore respiration or ATP production, is what makes this arm the leading explanation for the treatment resistance of the cardiac phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Echocardiography studies corroborated a DCM phenotype with significantly reduced ejection fraction and left ventricular dilation similar to those seen in individuals with PGM1-CDG.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the convergent dilated-cardiomyopathy readout and its fidelity to the human phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Our findings also suggest that the autosomal recessive PGM1-CDG might be highly associated with life-threatening cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia or sudden cardiac death as the first symptom presenting from childhood and adolescence.
evidence.explanation: Human evidence that the cardiac arm can be the presenting and fatal manifestation.

steps/11.description: The convergent cardiac consequence and the most life-threatening complication of PGM1-CDG. Ventricular dilation with a falling ejection fraction progresses to heart failure, arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, transplantation or sudden death. It is the one manifestation D-galactose does not correct, which is why it is modeled as a distinct convergence node fed by two competing upstream arms rather than folded into the general multisystem outflow.

evidence.snippet: Symptoms typically start in infancy and most frequently include hypoglycemia (possibly leading to seizures), cleft palate/bifid uvula (which can lead to feeding difficulties), elevated liver enzymes, coagulopathy, muscle weakness and exercise intolerance (often with rhabdomyolysis), and, in some cases, cardiomyopathy
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the multisystem consequence set downstream of hypoglycosylation. Tagged OTHER because this is an expert review summarizing the phenotype rather than reporting primary data.

evidence.snippet: Four out of seven patients have deteriorating adrenal function with abnormally low cortisol and ACTH levels during hypoglycemia and subnormal response of cortisol to low dose ACTH test
evidence.explanation: Documents the endocrine (ACTH/cortisol axis) component of the multisystem glycoprotein dysfunction.

steps/12.description: Simultaneous hypoglycosylation of many secreted and membrane glycoproteins produces the characteristic multisystem outflow: hepatic dysfunction with transaminase elevation, endocrine deficits (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, secondary adrenal insufficiency, growth failure), craniofacial malformation, and variable neurologic involvement, in addition to the coagulation and cardiac arms modeled separately.

evidence.snippet: The most frequently observed abnormality was AT (mean: 30.8% R:80-120 %) deficiency. Four individuals had major thrombotic events.
evidence.explanation: Identifies antithrombin as the dominant coagulation abnormality and documents clinically significant thrombosis.

steps/13.description: Coagulation and anticoagulation proteins are heavily glycosylated and are among the most sensitive readouts of hypoglycosylation in CDG. In PGM1-CDG antithrombin is the most commonly and most severely affected factor, with prolonged aPTT and reductions in factors XI, IX and VII also reported; a minority of patients suffer major thrombotic events. These abnormalities improve on D-galactose, making antithrombin activity a candidate treatment biomarker and trial endpoint.

evidence.snippet: After a dietary glucose load, large amounts of glucose-6-phosphate are generated, which cannot be converted into glycogen.
evidence.explanation: Explains the postprandial diversion of hexose phosphate that accompanies the fasting-intolerance phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Recurrent episodes of ketotic hypoglycemia were present in 6/7 patients.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the fasting hypoglycemia phenotype within a single well characterized family.

evidence.snippet: Hypoglycemia was primarily due to hyperinsulinism in young patients.
evidence.explanation: The international guideline establishes hyperinsulinism as the primary route to hypoglycemia in young patients, correcting a prior description that treated it as only an unspecified subset finding.

steps/14.description: Because hepatic glycogen cannot be released as glucose through the PGM1 step, fasting, intercurrent illness, or vomiting precipitate ketotic hypoglycemia, frequently the presenting problem in infancy. Conversely, after a glucose load, accumulating glucose-6-phosphate that cannot be stored as glycogen is diverted toward lactate and lipogenesis, contributing to transaminase elevation and hepatic steatosis. In young patients, hypoglycemia is primarily hyperinsulinemic, whereas starvation- or febrile-illness-associated ketotic hypoglycemia is also reported and becomes more relevant at other ages. Secondary ACTH/cortisol deficiency can further compound the hypoglycemia.

evidence.snippet: Signs of hepatopathy with moderately elevated serum aminotransferase levels developed in all patients.
evidence.explanation: "in all patients" in the 19-patient landmark cohort supports the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/15.description: Moderately elevated serum aminotransferases are near-universal in the multisystem form and often prompt the diagnostic workup. Hepatic steatosis and hepatomegaly are also reported. Importantly, hepatic involvement is characteristically absent in the primary myopathic form, so this phenotype is scoped to the multisystem subtype rather than asserted disease-wide.

evidence.snippet: Episodes of acute hepatic failure were described in five patients, however, without details concerning the circumstances or the extent of presentation.
evidence.explanation: Five of the 57 molecularly confirmed patients reviewed by the guideline falls in the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/16.description: Acute hepatic failure has occurred in a minority of patients and did not correlate with overall phenotypic severity. This acute risk complements the more typical chronic or intermittent transaminase elevation.

evidence.snippet: Hypoglycemia was common, especially in childhood, requiring treatment with frequent meals, complex carbohydrates, or overnight tube feeding.
evidence.explanation: "common" maps to the FREQUENT band per the project frequency-mapping table.

evidence.snippet: Recurrent episodes of ketotic hypoglycemia were present in 6/7 patients.
evidence.explanation: Documents the recurrent, ketotic character of the hypoglycemia.

steps/17.description: Fasting or illness-associated ketotic hypoglycemia is common, especially in childhood, and may be severe enough to provoke seizures. Management requires frequent complex-carbohydrate meals, an emergency illness plan, and in some patients overnight enteral feeding. Coexisting hyperinsulinism or secondary adrenal insufficiency can aggravate it.

evidence.snippet: The majority of the patients had muscle symptoms, including exercise intolerance, muscle weakness, and rhabdomyolysis.
evidence.explanation: "The majority of the patients" maps to the FREQUENT band (30-79%).

steps/18.description: Exercise intolerance, exertional fatigue and muscle tightness reflect the inability to mobilize muscle glycogen for anaerobic energy production. Patients show a McArdle-like second wind and an absent lactate response to ischemic forearm exercise. This may be the only manifestation in adult-onset presentations.

evidence.snippet: Attacks of rhabdomyolysis were studied in 43 patients and occurred in 25% of patients (11/43).
evidence.explanation: The guideline's phenotype-specific denominator places rhabdomyolysis at 25%, supporting OCCASIONAL and superseding the earlier over-read of a compound sentence about muscle symptoms overall.

steps/19.description: Episodic rhabdomyolysis, typically triggered by exertion or intercurrent illness, with elevated creatine kinase. Two patients in the landmark cohort developed malignant hyperthermia with severe rhabdomyolysis after general anesthesia, so anesthetic risk requires specific attention.

evidence.snippet: The majority of the patients had muscle symptoms, including exercise intolerance, muscle weakness, and rhabdomyolysis.
evidence.explanation: Muscle weakness is one of the muscle symptoms present in the majority of the landmark cohort, supporting the FREQUENT band.

steps/20.description: Proximal and generalized muscle weakness accompanies the exercise intolerance; in the adult-onset myopathic presentation it may be the only manifestation. One reported patient had fluctuating weakness with electrophysiological evidence of neuromuscular junction involvement.

evidence.snippet: Dilated cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrest, or both occurred in six patients; three patients were listed for heart transplantation.
evidence.explanation: 6/19 patients (about 32%) had dilated cardiomyopathy and/or cardiac arrest; the dilated cardiomyopathy subset alone is below that, supporting a conservative OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: Some patients develop life-threatening cardiomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: International consensus confirms the cardiomyopathy risk and its life-threatening character.

steps/21.description: Dilated cardiomyopathy is the most severe and most treatment-resistant manifestation. Onset ranges from infancy to adulthood; it may progress rapidly to heart failure, cardiac arrest, transplantation, or sudden death, and it is the leading cause of mortality in PGM1-CDG. Crucially, it does not improve on D-galactose, so lifelong cardiac surveillance is required even in biochemically well-controlled patients.

evidence.snippet: During follow-up one of the brothers died unexpectedly after physical exertion during daily life at the age of twelve years.
evidence.explanation: Documents exertion-associated sudden death in a molecularly confirmed PGM1-CDG sibling.

steps/22.description: Sudden cardiac death, sometimes after physical exertion and sometimes as the first manifestation of the disorder, has been documented in PGM1-CDG siblings, which motivates cardiac evaluation and genetic testing in unexplained sudden death in the young.

evidence.snippet: Other echocardiogram abnormalities include mild left ventricular enlargement (n = 3), septal defects (n = 2), and valvular heart defects (n = 2).
evidence.explanation: Three of 57 patients (5.3%) had mild left-ventricular enlargement, supporting the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/23.description: Mild left-ventricular enlargement can occur as a structural cardiac finding in addition to overt dilated cardiomyopathy.

evidence.snippet: Coagulation information was available for only 58.9 % of the reported individuals, out of which 67.4 % of PGM1-CDG individuals were reported to have abnormalities. The most frequently observed abnormality was AT (mean: 30.8% R:80-120 %) deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Among the 58.9% of reported individuals for whom coagulation data existed, 67.4% had abnormalities and antithrombin was the most frequent. The band is therefore stated on the tested denominator, not the whole reported cohort; the 67.4% figure covers any coagulation abnormality rather than antithrombin deficiency specifically, so FREQUENT is the most that this evidence supports.

steps/24.description: Antithrombin deficiency is the most frequent coagulation abnormality in PGM1-CDG, with mean activity around 31% against a reference range of 80-120%. It improves substantially on D-galactose and is a leading candidate treatment biomarker.

evidence.snippet: Four individuals had major thrombotic events.
evidence.explanation: Four major thrombotic events among 73 reported individuals (about 5%) supports the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/25.description: Major thrombotic events occur in a minority of patients, consistent with the profound antithrombin deficiency; peri-operative bleeding and thrombosis risk should both be assessed before surgery.

evidence.snippet: Growth retardation was reported in all but four patients.
evidence.explanation: 15/19 patients (about 79%) reported with growth retardation, at the top of the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: 4/7 have short stature (<-2 SDS) and one was diagnosed with growth hormone deficiency
evidence.explanation: Independent series quantifying short stature specifically (rather than "growth retardation") at 4/7, and documenting growth hormone deficiency as one contributing mechanism.

steps/26.description: Growth retardation is reported in the large majority of patients; growth hormone deficiency has been documented in individual cases.

evidence.snippet: Decreased levels of growth hormone or IGF1 was reported in 12 patients
evidence.explanation: The combined growth-hormone/IGF-1 count is 12/57 (21%), supporting the OCCASIONAL band for axis deficiency. Indirect because the source pools growth hormone and IGF-1 measurements and does not report how many patients had reduced growth hormone specifically.

evidence.snippet: 9 patients showed decreased serum insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3)
evidence.explanation: Adds evidence for the IGFBP-3 component of the growth-hormone/IGF axis; indirect for the bound growth-hormone term because it measures a different analyte on the same axis.

steps/27.description: Reduced growth hormone or IGF-1 and reduced IGFBP-3 identify an endocrine contribution to growth impairment in a subset of patients. The available count combines several measurements along the growth-hormone axis; the bound term covers the growth-hormone component, and the IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 components are described here in prose. The prior binding to Secondary growth hormone deficiency asserted a secondary (hypothalamic-pituitary) origin that the sources do not establish.

evidence.snippet: Two girls had hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with delayed puberty.
evidence.explanation: 2/19 patients (about 11%) maps to the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/28.description: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with delayed puberty has been reported; notably it resolved within weeks of starting galactose supplementation in two affected girls, with rising LH and normalizing FSH.

evidence.snippet: ACTH deficiency should be considered in any PGM1 deficient patient with hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Recommends screening for ACTH deficiency. The OCCASIONAL band is set conservatively because 4/7 in a single consanguineous family is not generalizable to the wider PGM1-CDG population.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, seven patients presented with hypocortisolism and five of them had increased adrenocorticotropic hormone levels.
evidence.explanation: The guideline's literature synthesis documents hypocortisolism with raised ACTH in most of the reported patients, a pattern pointing away from a purely ACTH-deficient (secondary) mechanism and motivating the general adrenal insufficiency binding.

steps/29.description: Secondary (ACTH-dependent) adrenal insufficiency, with inappropriately low cortisol and ACTH during hypoglycemia and a subnormal low-dose ACTH stimulation test, was found in more than half of one well-characterized family and should be actively sought in any PGM1-deficient patient with hypoglycemia. The consensus guideline separately reports hypocortisolism with raised ACTH in most affected patients across the literature, so the site of the axis defect is not uniform and the general adrenal insufficiency term is deliberately retained over a secondary-specific one.

evidence.snippet: High levels of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) were reported in three patients and decreased levels of thyroxin-binding globulin (TBG) in six.
evidence.explanation: Elevated TSH in 3/57 patients (5.3%) supports the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/30.description: Elevated TSH is a documented thyroid-axis abnormality. Clinical hypothyroidism should be treated with L-thyroxine, while TSH, free T4 and thyroxine-binding globulin are monitored longitudinally.

evidence.snippet: Epileptic seizures have been reported in three patients with developmental delay, with an abnormal EEG detected in one patient.
evidence.explanation: Seizures in 3/57 patients (5.3%) support the OCCASIONAL band and provide a specific HPO association in place of the prior neurologic umbrella term.

steps/31.description: Seizures have been reported with developmental delay and may be primary or secondary to hypoglycemia.

evidence.snippet: The most common clinical presentations include muscle involvement, failure to thrive, cleft palate, and cardiac involvement.
evidence.explanation: Lists failure to thrive among the most common presenting features across 73 reported individuals.

steps/32.description: Failure to thrive, often compounded by feeding difficulty from cleft palate and by recurrent hypoglycemia, is among the most common presenting features.

edges/2.description: Loss of enzyme activity directly removes the catalytic step that interconverts the two hexose phosphates.

edges/3.description: Glycogen can neither be built from glucose-6-phosphate nor mobilized into glycolysis, because both routes require the PGM1 step.

edges/4.description: Reduced glucose-1-phosphate availability limits UDP-glucose synthesis, the donor pool feeding endoplasmic-reticulum glycan assembly.

edges/5.description: The Leloir pathway is functionally stalled, lowering the UDP-galactose pool needed for Golgi galactosylation.

edges/8.description: The same inability to route glycogen-derived carbon into glycolysis compromises cardiomyocyte energy supply. This is arm (a) of the galactose-resistant-cardiomyopathy hypothesis.

edges/9.description: Incompletely assembled precursors produce whole missing N-glycans, the type I component of the transferrin pattern.

edges/10.description: Incomplete Golgi galactosylation yields truncated, galactose-deficient glycans, the type II component of the transferrin pattern.

edges/13.description: Sarcolemmal and extracellular-matrix glycoproteins, notably laminin subunits, are hypoglycosylated in the myocardium. This is arm (b) of the galactose-resistant-cardiomyopathy hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Abnormal baseline results (alanine transaminase, aspartate transaminase, activated partial thromboplastin time) improved or normalized already using 1 g/kg/day D-gal.
evidence.explanation: Correction of the transaminase elevation by restoring nucleotide sugars supports a glycosylation contribution to the hepatopathy; the rescue is indirect evidence for the forward causal claim.

edges/14.description: Hepatic dysfunction is part of the glycoprotein outflow, alongside the metabolic arm modeled on the fasting-hypoglycemia node; transaminases improve or normalize on D-galactose, tying this arm of the hepatopathy to glycosylation.

edges/15.description: Growth failure follows from the growth hormone-IGF axis deficiency of the endocrine arm together with chronic multisystem disease; the axis deficiency is recorded as its own phenotype.

edges/16.description: Reduced growth hormone/IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 identify an endocrine lesion within the multisystem glycoprotein outflow; which client glycoproteins of the axis are responsible has not been established.

evidence.snippet: two of them presented with delayed puberty and decreased serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). In both patients, d-galactose supplementation (0.5–1.0 g/kg/day) resolved both features.
evidence.explanation: Resolution of the hypogonadism when nucleotide sugars are replenished ties it to the glycosylation arm; a treatment response is indirect evidence for the forward causal claim.

edges/17.description: The gonadotropins are glycoprotein hormones, and the hypogonadism resolves on D-galactose together with the glycosylation defect.

edges/18.description: Adrenal dysfunction is part of the endocrine outflow of the multisystem glycoprotein lesion, but the site of the axis defect differs between reports (low ACTH with low cortisol in one family, hypocortisolism with raised ACTH in other patients), so the intermediate mechanism is unknown.

evidence.snippet: Liver enzymes, thyroid hormones, and coagulation factors normalize on long term d-galactose therapy and are easily monitored, while blood sugar levels might fluctuate regardless of d-galactose therapy.
evidence.explanation: Normalization of thyroid hormones on D-galactose ties the thyroid-axis abnormality to the glycosylation arm; a treatment response is indirect evidence for the forward causal claim.

edges/19.description: Thyroid-axis abnormalities (raised TSH, reduced thyroxine-binding globulin) accompany the glycosylation defect and normalize on long-term D-galactose; the specific client glycoprotein responsible is not established.

edges/20.description: Feeding difficulty from the palatal malformation, recurrent hypoglycemia and chronic hepatic and endocrine dysfunction converge on failure to thrive in infancy; the intermediates are modeled elsewhere in the entry.

edges/21.description: Antithrombin is the most frequently and most severely affected client glycoprotein of the coagulation arm; its activity improves on D-galactose in parallel with glycosylation.

evidence.snippet: The most frequently observed abnormality was AT (mean: 30.8% R:80-120 %) deficiency. Four individuals had major thrombotic events.
evidence.explanation: The cohort reports the thrombotic events alongside the profound antithrombin deficiency; attributing them to antithrombin loss is the recognized consequence of that deficiency rather than a per-patient demonstrated sequence, so the quote bears on the edge indirectly.

edges/22.description: Loss of antithrombin anticoagulant activity predisposes to the major thrombotic events reported in a minority of patients.

edges/23.description: Fasting or intercurrent illness precipitates hypoglycemia because hepatic glycogen cannot be released as glucose through the blocked PGM1 step.

edges/24.description: Postprandial diversion of unstorable glucose-6-phosphate toward lactate and lipogenesis contributes to transaminase elevation and hepatic steatosis, the metabolic arm of the hepatopathy.

edges/25.description: Episodes of acute hepatic failure occur in a minority of patients on the background of this chronic hepatic metabolic stress; the consensus guideline reports the episodes without details of their precipitating circumstances, so the intermediate steps are unknown.

evidence.snippet: Seizures can be primary or secondary to hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: The guideline states the hypoglycemia-to-seizure route directly while acknowledging that primary seizures also occur, which is why this edge explains only part of the seizure phenotype.

edges/26.description: Hypoglycemic episodes can provoke seizures. Primary, non-hypoglycemic seizures are also reported and are covered by the neurodevelopmental knowledge gap rather than by this edge.

edges/27.description: Inability to mobilize muscle glycogen for rapid anaerobic ATP production produces exertional fatigue and tightness, the absent lactate response, and the McArdle-like second wind.

edges/28.description: Chronic energy failure in skeletal muscle manifests as proximal and generalized weakness, which may be the only manifestation in the adult-onset myopathic form.

edges/29.description: Exertion or intercurrent illness outstrips the energy supply of glycogenolysis-blocked muscle, producing episodic myocyte breakdown with elevated creatine kinase.

evidence.snippet: Our data suggests PGM1 is key regulator of cardiomyocyte function, linking sarcomeric Z-disk integrity with mitochondrial metabolism.
evidence.explanation: The authors state the Z-disk-to-mitochondrion link as a suggestion from correlated proteomic and respirometry findings, not as a demonstrated causal sequence, so this edge is indirect and its intermediates are unknown.

edges/32.description: Loss of Z-disk-mitochondrial coupling is the proposed route from sarcomeric destabilization to the energetic failure of the myocyte.

evidence.snippet: PGM1-deficient iCMs exhibited reduced beating frequency, impaired contractility, and prolonged contraction kinetics.
evidence.explanation: Functional contractile deficit measured directly in the patient-derived cardiomyocyte model.

edges/33.description: Impaired contractility and prolonged contraction kinetics in PGM1-deficient cardiomyocytes are the cellular correlate of the clinical cardiomyopathy.

edges/34.description: The clinical phenotype of this convergence node: ventricular dilation with a falling ejection fraction progressing to heart failure, transplantation or death.

edges/35.description: Mild left-ventricular enlargement is the milder echocardiographic readout of the same myocardial disease process.

edges/36.description: Arrhythmia, cardiac arrest and exertion-associated sudden death are documented outcomes of the cardiomyopathy, sometimes as the first manifestation of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: We identified 21 different mutations in PGM1 in 19 patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PGM1 as the causal gene and documents substantial allelic heterogeneity.

evidence.snippet: Regression analysis showed that there is no significant correlation between genotype, enzyme activity, and TPCRS score.
evidence.explanation: Supports the absence of a usable genotype-phenotype correlation in PGM1-CDG.

genes/0.notes: PGM1 (1p31.3) encodes cytosolic phosphoglucomutase-1.
